articles.title: France braces for fresh unrest, government vows tough response
articles.summary: Some 150 gatherings are planned across France, the interior ministry says

blocks.text: POLICE PREPARATIONS. French gendarmerie and police officers gather near Arc de Triomphe on the day of a demonstration organized by labor unions as part of nationwide protests called by the 'Yellow Vests' movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 31, 2026.
Pedro Nunes/Reuters
Some 150 gatherings are planned across France, the interior ministry says

items: France has deployed 70,000 police to manage expected protests on October 31, driven by public anger over living costs and President Macron's government.
A ban on a major march in Paris has been enforced, with authorities concerned about potential rioters using Halloween masks to hide their identities.
The unrest has led to significant economic losses and has bolstered far-right political sentiments ahead of upcoming elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

PARIS, France – France deployed a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday, October 31, in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.

The demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings, and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.

“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying “a very high risk” of unrest.

France’s top administrative court confirmed on Saturday a march between the emblematic Paris squares of Republique and Bastille will be banned, rejecting a challenge by unions. Demonstrations will instead have to be held on boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, away from the main shopping areas in central Paris.

Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
Some 150 gatherings were planned across France, the interior ministry said.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.

The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.

Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair, have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent “Yellow Vest” movement demanding action on the cost of living.
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.

“When I was little, I was told young people were the future,” said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
“Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing.”

The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.

Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton, and Burberry.

The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump beware: US voters are concerned about government corruption
articles.summary: Alleged self-dealing by the president and his allies doesn’t look so good as corruption emerges as a key issue for midterm voters

blocks.text: Voters under 50 probably won’t remember the “welfare queen”. But she once embodied Republicans’ claim of the underlying reason for US societal decay: the poor are a bunch of fraudsters.

Ronald Reagan introduced Linda Taylor to US voters at a rally during the Republican presidential primary season in 1976. A resident of Chicago’s South Side, Taylor had been arrested for welfare fraud. “She used 80 names, 30 addresses, five phone numbers to collect food stamps, social security, veteran’s benefits for four non-existing deceased veteran husbands,” Reagan said. “Her tax-free cash income alone has been running $150,000 a year.”

Taylor may have committed crimes worse than social security fraud. But she wasn’t living on anything near $150,000. Josh Levin, author of The Queen: The Forgotten Life Behind an American Myth, points out that she was only ever charged with stealing $9,000. And yet, Reagan leveraged Taylor’s story to slash spending on welfare, food stamps, Medicaid, public housing and job training.

This woman of color on the bottom rungs of society – born out of a forbidden encounter in the deep south between a white mother and a black father – justified the proposition that to weed out corruption, the first place to look was among the (nonwhite) poor.

Half a century on, the Trump administration is dipping into the old imagery to buttress a violent campaign against what’s left of the US’s social safety net, and distract voters from the industrial-scale corruption that is, indeed, sinking America: the self-dealing by the president, his family and his friends.

Pages from Reagan’s 1980s playbook are being used to justify initiatives to eviscerate the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap), and government-subsidized health insurance by claiming fraud by less fortunate Americans who, evidently, are learned in the art of grift.

The most recent discovery, announced by JD Vance’s anti-fraud taskforce, amounted to $40m defrauded from Snap. “There are people out there who decide to commit fraud against these programs who, quite literally in this case, will steal from the mouths of hungry children in order to enrich themselves,” the vice-president said in Ohio.

This came on the heels of Vance’s gleeful announcement that the administration had nixed the health coverage of 760,000 people insured under Obamacare on grounds of fraud. And it meshed nicely with Donald Trump’s offer of a bounty to whoever catches moochers grifting off the government’s dime. “If you turn somebody in, and you, let’s say, report, and you find $1bn, we are giving a commission to that person of 1%,” he said.

Trump probably thinks this is smart politics. But Americans are becoming alarmed over the corruption popping up all over the news. An October Harris poll for the Guardian found that government corruption is the second most important issue for voters heading to the polls, second only to the rising cost of living. Eighty-seven percent of respondents to the poll said corruption was a problem, a greater share than those worried about AI or immigration.

And yet there’s a hole in the president’s logic. Voters, according to the Harris poll, don’t seem too worried about people getting health insurance on the sly. They are worried about “elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public”. Trump making billions off of crypto would probably fit that concern.

Vance has tried to address that complication. He claimed: “I have not seen a single shred of evidence that he participates or sanctions in that corruption.” Vance reminded the electorate that “this guy was a billionaire before he ever got into politics,” which in the vice-president’s mind probably limits Trump’s incentive to stick his hand in the cookie jar.
The 65% of voters planning to vote in the midterms who think this corruption is a “major problem”, are unlikely to buy that, though.

Last year, the US ranked as the 29th least corrupt nation on the Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index, a notch below its rank in the last year of the Biden administration and down from 18th in 2016, the year before Trump first came into office. Vance might want to read up on that. Or he might just open his eyes.

Trump making $2.2bn in his first year back in office, including $1.4bn from crypto, may not amount to corruption in the narrow sense preferred by his allies on the supreme court, who granted him immunity for any act that might be considered “official”. Trump might not have received direct bribes or agreed to a specific quid pro quo, offering to change policy in exchange for cash.

But, just for instance, Trump’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) paused a lawsuit for fraud against a crypto billionaire who had bought $40m worth of $Trump meme coins and invested $75m in another Trump crypto business. Trump nixed the team at the justice department that investigated illegal uses of crypto, and dropped investigations into a variety of crypto companies, including Coinbase, Ripple and Kraken, that contributed to his campaign.
after newsletter promotion

The Trump Organization, led by his son Eric, has been cutting deals left and right with regimes that have an indisputable interest in Trump’s foreign policy. A Vladimir Putin-connected oligarch financed a wedding party on a private island for the president’s son, Donald Jr. And Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is cutting billion-dollar deals with the rulers of countries with which he is conducting diplomacy on behalf of the US.
The Democratic congresswoman Rosa DeLauro has compiled a helpful list of the many ways Trump is enriching himself, his family and his allies while in office. It includes:

items: The Qatari government gifted him a luxury jet, potentially violating the emoluments clause of the constitution.

The UAE gained access to some tightly guarded, high-end American AI chips soon after an investment firm linked to its ruling family secretly bought a $500m stake in World Liberty Financial, the crypto company funded by the families of Trump and his chum Steve Witkoff.

Rich people facing criminal charges have taken to donating to Trump’s political operations and then seeking pardons or clemency. Most recently, Wanda Vázquez Garced, the former governor of Puerto Rico, and the banker who paid her bribes, Julio Herrera Velutini, were pardoned after Velutini’s family gave a $50m deal to Alina Habba, Trump’s former personal lawyer, and donated $3.5m to Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac.

The first family is also making a killing from the government. The Pentagon lent more than $600m to Vulcan Elements, a rare earths startup, just three months after Donald Jr’s venture capital firm 1789 Capital bought a stake in the outfit.

Powerus, a drone maker backed by Eric and Donald Jr is selling drone interceptors to Persian Gulf allies of the US that are under attack by Iran, enriching the kids from a misbegotten war launched by the dad without consulting Congress.

blocks.text: A British researcher has also built an online tracker documenting hundreds of acts of corruption and abuse of office during Trump’s last 21 months in the White House.
The White House denies that the Trump family has ever engaged in any conflicts of interest, and denies granting any pardons or clemency in exchange for political donations.

Reagan may have been happy to cut poor Americans adrift. But he wasn’t in it for personal gain. Trump, by contrast, seems to think that going after moochers abusing Snap, offering Maga loyalists a bounty to catch a few, will distract voters from his efforts to leverage his office for cash.
Here’s to hoping that US voters – even those inclined to buy into images of undeserving “welfare queens” defrauding government aid programs – can recognize real corruption when they see it.

articles.title: Number of unqualified Nunavut teachers nearly doubled in 5 years
articles.summary: The number of teachers who have letters of authority in Nunavut classrooms has nearly doubled in 5 years, from around 50 to now over 90. Nunavut's education minister David Akeeagok says he's not…

image.caption: Nunavut Education Minister David Akeeagok says he's not concerned with the number of teachers who have one-year letters of authority allowing them to teach in Nunavut's schools. The teachers' union says it is worried, and is warning of the territory's growing reliance on unqualified teachers. (Camer

blocks.text: North

The number of teachers who have letters of authority in Nunavut classrooms has nearly doubled in 5 years, from around 50 to now over 90. Nunavut's education minister David Akeeagok says he's not concerned about the increase, but the teachers’ union warns of the growing reliance on unqualified teachers.
Nunavut's education minister says he's not concerned about the increase
Nunavut Education Minister David Akeeagok said he isn’t worried about the number of unqualified teachers in classrooms, even though it has almost doubled in five years.
“We're not concerned,” he said. "There's over 800 [teachers], and 93 is a small number of the percentage, and it's reflective of the need for us to make sure the school operates."

Those 93 teachers work under what are called "letters of authority." These are issued for one-year terms by the Department of Education when a position can't be filled by a qualified teacher with a bachelor's degree in education or equivalent.
The number of teachers in Nunavut with letters of authority has steadily increased each year for the past five years, nearly doubling.
In 2021-22, there were more than 50 unqualified teachers. Now, that's up to 93 for 2025-26.
Nunavut Teachers' Association president Justin Matchett disagrees with Akeeagok's assessment of the issue. He said the increase is a problem.

"That's 10 per cent of our membership [that] is unqualified. So it is a concern of ours,” he said. “We rely heavily on these unqualified teachers, on the letter of authority teachers. We can't operate the schools without them."
Akeeagok attributes the steady increase to the teacher shortage across the country.

items: Nunavut schools lack teachers as year begins. Without housing, some say that won’t change

blocks.text: He said Nunavut Arctic College's education program has been training many local teachers in communities. Some teachers who formerly worked under letters of authority are now getting certified, he said.
“We want to attract as many local teachers as we can,” he said. “We're looking forward to those graduates to become teachers in their communities.”
Number of unqualified teachers in Nunavut classrooms nearly doubles in 5 years
Teachers’ union concerned about increase
Matchett argues the shortage of qualified teachers has been going on too long.

“When I first started, a letter of authority was usually held for our language specialist,” he said. “Now the letter of authority is definitely used a lot more due to the teaching shortage and it's covering everything from classroom teachers to the language specialist.”
Ultimately, Matchett said, this is about the children and the quality of education they are getting.

"As a parent, if I know that one Grade 3 [classroom] that my daughter is in has an unqualified teacher and the other class has a qualified teacher, I'd be concerned about the level of education," he said.
Across Canada, Matchett said, there are just not enough students in education programs to fill the number of vacancies that are opening every year. (Cameron Lane/CBC)

The Department of Education does offer orientation and professional development training for letter of authority teachers. Akeeagok said right now these teachers are undergoing training sessions, with another one planned for the new year.
"Our department is very committed in ensuring that we get qualified teachers. When that doesn't happen, we need to resort to letters of authority," Akeeagok said.
Matchett said he’s aware and happy that letter of authority teachers get professional development opportunities, but the teachers’ union isn’t involved in what is being taught or what the content is.
With Nunavut slowly rolling out a new curriculum, he stressed the importance of ensuring teachers — qualified or unqualified — are trained consistently year after year.

“Somebody could be in a letter of authority position right now, receiving that training on the new curriculum, and then not be back next year,” he said. “Who's going to train that new teacher on the curriculum? So it's just that cycle, right?”

items: Nunavut’s new school curriculum ‘going well’ 1 year in, education minister says

blocks.text: In Nunavut, Matchett said there’s a teacher retention problem, with many educators leaving the profession. But he said filling the gaps with unqualified teachers is not a long-term solution.
“What's the ultimate goal here? We can't keep relying on them and it's not a fail safe,” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Bianca McKeown is a reporter with CBC North in Iqaluit. Previously, she worked at CBC Ottawa. Have a story idea? Email her at: bianca.mckeown@cbc.ca

articles.title: Massive Gen Z protests set to sweep cities across Germany
articles.summary: Young people in Germany are taking to the streets in some 34 cities, calling for greater political say and a more hopeful future. The protests come amid a wave of youth demonstrations across Europe.…

image.caption: Despite the protest organizers rejecting violence, some shop owners have taken precautions, like seen here in Berlin Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Young people in Germany are taking to the streets in some 34 cities, calling for greater political say and a more hopeful future. The protests come amid a wave of youth demonstrations across Europe. DW has more.
Prefer DW on Google

blocks.caption: Despite the protest organizers rejecting violence, some shop owners have taken precautions, like seen here in Berlin Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Organizers of mass youth protests on Saturday hope that more than 170,000 people will take part in some 34 cities
Protesters are to call for more money for schools, measures to lower the cost of living, greater social justice and more climate protection
They will also protest at the possible reintroduction of military conscription
The protests come as young people across Europe take a stand for their rights in several countries, notably in France
Security authorities say they have no evidence of any planned violence, but the Interior Ministry has warned that extremists might hijack the protests

blocks.text: This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31, 2026:
October 31, 2026
German 'Gen Z' protests set for cities across the country

blocks.caption: A youth protester holds a sign during a demonstration in September reading: 'social services instead of conscription' [FILE SEPTEMBER 2026]Image: Sven Kaeuler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Young people are to take part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday, following the example of their peers in France and other countries who have been calling for better educational prospects and future opportunities.
In Germany, organizers said there is also to be a focus on rejecting military conscription and on demanding more protection for the climate as the Earth warms, with potentially catastrophic effects.
Saturday's protests are being called for by the youth initiative "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") through a social media campaign
The group itself will directly organize four of the protests — in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich —, with associated demonstrations to take place in some 30 other cities.
It has explicitly called for peaceful protests without the violence that marred recent demonstrations in France.
Focus on security fears
This has not stopped several conservative politicians, notably from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), from warning that similar scenes could occur.
"Gen Z regelt" has, however, criticized what it sees as a wrong focus on the possibility of violence at the protests.

"It shows that our point about not being taken seriously or being heard is right. No one wants to work with us on the issues at stake but instead always put the topic of violence on the agenda," an organizer of the Munich protest told a press conference in Cologne.
However, other lawmakers have come out in support of the protests.

The leader of the parliamentary party of the Greens, Katharina Dröge, told the DPA news agency: "Young people are rightly furious because the federal government does not take their wishes seriously enough."
The Left Party leader, Luigi Pantisano, also said it was the right time for protests as the government mulls reforms of the nursing care and pensions systems, calling them "social cruelties."
"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1997 and 2012.

articles.title: Over 60,000 passengers leave ports for Undas — PCG
articles.summary: More than 60,000 passengers have departed from ports nationwide as Filipinos travel for the observance of Undas 2026, the Philippine Coast Guard said.

blocks.text: October 31, 2026 | 5:30pm
The Philippine Coast Guard monitors passenger movement at the Port of Ormoc City on Oct. 31, 2026,
Philippine Coast Guard via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — More than 60,000 passengers have departed from ports nationwide as Filipinos travel for the observance of Undas 2026, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.

Based on data posted on the PCG's official Facebook page on Saturday, October 31, the agency recorded 60,411 outbound passengers and 54,291 inbound passengers across ports nationwide from noon to 6 p.m. on Saturday, October 31.
To ensure passenger safety and smooth port operations, the agency deployed 6,221 frontline personnel from its 17 districts.
Coast Guard personnel also inspected 540 vessels and 806 motorbancas as part of its preparations for the expected increase in passenger traffic during the holiday period.
The PCG placed all its districts, stations and substations on heightened alert from October 29 to November 3 to monitor port operations and assist travelers.
The agency said the measures aim to ensure safe and efficient travel as more passengers head to their provinces and other destinations for the observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day.

articles.title: Cost of living protests to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween
articles.summary:
Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing

Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite…
articles.byline: Deborah Cole in Berlin and Jon Henley in Paris

blocks.text: Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.

Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.

blocks.caption: Students and activists block access to the Andreas-Gymnasium in Berlin this month in protest against compulsory military service and education cuts. Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.

“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.

blocks.caption: A Gen Z regelt poster in Leipzig announcing a protest on Saturday at Augustusplatz. Photograph: Maria Castro/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.
Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”
By Friday, more than 160,000 people had registered on the website saying they planned to attend the protests.

The federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.
It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on the marked decline in German school performance.
after newsletter promotion

In France, the interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.

Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.

“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities ‌across France,” he said.

The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.

blocks.caption: Protesters holding a French flag amid clashes during demonstrations in Paris last Saturday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters

blocks.text: Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.

In Paris, two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. An appeal by organisers against the decision to exclude them from the centre was rejected late on Friday night.

The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.

Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.

Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

articles.title: ‘Hope and help’: How the Philippines fights to lower breast cancer deaths
articles.summary: While treatments for late-stage breast cancer have reached the Philippines, medical professionals point out that making them available is vastly different from making them affordable and accessible

items: Global cancer research aims to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death, with advancements making metastatic breast cancer more manageable.
In the Philippines, breast cancer is often diagnosed at advanced stages due to misconceptions and lack of awareness, leading to poorer outcomes compared to countries like the US.
Efforts are being made to improve early detection and access to treatment through government programs and community initiatives, but significant gaps remain in awareness and accessibility.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – There’s a bold ambition in global cancer research to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death.

And it’s this goal that has transformed cancer treatment over the years, even making Stage 4 or metastatic breast cancer — when the cancer has spread to distant organs like the bones, lungs, liver, or brain — more manageable.

“It’s important for people to know that metastatic breast cancer is not a death sentence,” said Dr. Marvin Mendoza, head of medical oncology and ambulatory infusion therapy unit of the National Kidney and Transplant Institute.
“It’s really very different from before, like the ’90s. We now have a lot of options.”
“The medical advancement in cancer is really fast. There’s a lot of investment in innovative medicine,” added Dr. Kriska Lim, medical affairs head of oncology for AstraZeneca Philippines.

“Most people think when it’s metastatic breast cancer, they won’t get treatment anymore. But even people with this cancer can live meaningful lives if they get the right treatment and the right support.”
But there are still a lot of hurdles doctors and breast cancer advocates face when dealing with Filipino patients.

For instance, some patients diagnosed at advanced stages abandon standard treatment and turn to alternative remedies, believing these will cure them. Others refuse biopsy on a suspected tumor, fearing the procedure will cause it to spread.

blocks.caption: Why are more Filipino women getting breast cancer?

blocks.text: Kara Magsanoc-Alikpala, co-founder of the ICanServe Foundation — which helps breast cancer patients by connecting them to medical specialists, educational resources, and support groups — said there are many misconceptions in local communities.
“Common ‘yung nakakahawa ang breast cancer (The belief that breast cancer is contagious is common). A lot of husbands distance themselves, it’s so common in communities,” she shared.
“There’s also the use of underwire bra and deodorants, we still get that. And the biopsy, ’pag ginalaw, kakalat (if moved, it might spread), it’s so common.”
The lack of breast cancer awareness and education remains one of the reasons the Philippines ranks poorly in global breast cancer statistics.

In the US, around 66% of breast cancer patients from 2019 to 2023 were “diagnosed at a localized stage, meaning the cancer had not spread outside the breast.” This early detection results in a higher survival rate, according to the United States Cancer Statistics.
Unfortunately, that isn’t the case in the Philippines.
“We’re so far from that. We’re the total opposite,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala. “Around 65% of breast cancer here is diagnosed at an advanced stage, Stage 3 or 4.”
Breast cancer remains the most common occurring cancer among Filipinos, according to the 2024 statistics of the International Agency for Research on Cancer of the World Health Organization (WHO).
It’s the second highest cause of death among Filipino cancer patients in both sexes at 12.9%, just behind lung cancer (13.6%).
In Asia, the Philippines also ranks in the top six for both breast cancer incidence and mortality in 2024, according to WHO.
“We really want breast cancer, and all cancers in general, to have enough attention. In AstraZeneca, our bold ambition is to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death,” said Lim.

“Recently, breast cancer is no longer the top cause of death. For it to happen, there’s a lot of things we have to look into. We recognize that it’s not enough that we bring the medicines in, it’s not enough that we invest. We’re supposed to work with like-minded organizations and really help the country move forward.”
“We do have advanced lines of treatment for metastatic breast cancer. It’s not just chemotherapy. There are a lot of targeted therapies now made available,” added Mendoza.

“Of course, made available is different from made affordable and accessible. But it’s one thing that they’re already here. We have to do the work to make it affordable for more patients, because treatment can take years or even a lifetime.“

blocks.caption: Rappler Talk: From breast cancer survivor to cancer exercise specialist

blocks.text: Medical professionals and advocates admit there are still many gaps even as the government expanded the PhilHealth Z Benefit, the health package that covers catastrophic and high-cost medical conditions.
“The biggest program is the PhilHealth Z Benefit package, but the sites and hospitals that offer it are still limited. That’s why the lines are so long,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

Other government programs to help alleviate medical costs include the YAKAP program, which covers cancer screening tests, and the Cancer Assistance Fund under the National Integrated Cancer Control Act, which covers specialized treatments and palliative care.
“There are many initiatives from the government, medical society, and private institutions, but it has to reach the communities. That’s the main barrier,” said Mendoza.
“If people don’t know about the program and initiatives, how to access them, it doesn’t complete the loop. There are still many people who haven’t been reached.”

While a lack of awareness about government programs often leads to late diagnosis and poorer outcomes, navigating the required paperwork once assistance is found presents an entirely different challenge.
“Kailangan pa rin ng kumpas ng gobyerno para mas ma-improve pa (The government needs to provide direction to improve it),” said Mendoza.
For now, some private institutions try to fill in the gaps, with the ICanServe Foundation, for instance, running its Ating Dibdibin (Take Your Breast Care to Heart) flagship program.
“We partner with local government, usually a city, then we institutionalize the program. It’s a community-based breast cancer control program with the aim of saving lives,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

“We bring services to the barangays instead of expecting them to go to the hospital. It’s proactive, going house to house, checking on women, because sometimes they don’t know where to go. We make sure there’s a clear pathway, there are patient navigators to hand-hold the patients.”

Lowering breast cancer deaths in the Philippines through early detection remains the key message among advocates, who hope that conversations would go beyond the Breast Cancer Awareness Month every October.
“The government should really have a national campaign. It’s the same message every year — early detection,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.
“We really need to be intentional in the way we promote our message, not only early detection, but there’s hope even if your cancer is diagnosed at a later stage.”
“I want everyone to know there’s hope and help,” she added.

“There’s the medical world, their supportive care. The government has some help — it’s not enough, but it’s a big help as well. There are foundations willing to help patients. But take charge of your health. Get screened. When you’re young, that’s the best time to find out.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Drug runner? Arms dealer? The Adeline-C made waves in Halifax and beyond
articles.summary: The Adeline-C arrived in Halifax on Oct. 31, 1981, filled with state-of-the-art equipment, but it was soon abandoned by its crew. It would be years before its role in a complex U.S. drug smuggling…

image.caption: The Adeline-C arrived in Halifax on Oct. 31, 1981. 'It was a really interesting story full of ... international intrigue and dope smuggling and big money," says Rob Gordon, a journalist who covered the ship. (www.newspapers.com)

blocks.text: Journalist Rob Gordon was at the courthouse on Upper Water Street in downtown Halifax one day in 1981 when he overheard a sheriff say something that piqued his interest.
"Oh, we were just on a boat, you know, and we seized a couple of guns and stuff," said one of the sheriffs.
Gordon, who later retired as a CBC News journalist, was covering courts then for the Chronicle-Herald newspaper.

On his lunch break, he headed down to the waterfront to check out the Adeline-C. The 32-metre trawler with a maximum width of seven metres had arrived in Halifax on Oct. 31, 1981, and was abandoned by most of the crew.

But it would be years later that the Adeline-C's role in a complex U.S. drug smuggling operation worth as much as $200 million US became fully known. Based out of the small coastal city of Newport, R.I., it involved purchasing around 100,000 pounds of marijuana and hash from the Middle East and Far East.
The operation was financed by a fraudulent bank loan in the Channel Islands that paid for the drugs, ships and manpower needed to run the scheme.

This Sept. 3, 2013, photo shows Guernsey, one of the Channel Islands in the waters between England and France. A loan was obtained from there due to the territory being an offshore tax haven. (Charmaine Noronha/The Associated Press)

Gordon found the ship tied up near Historic Properties. On board were two shady characters who had joined the ship in Florida and travelled north with it. Gordon knew them and they welcomed him aboard to have a look around.
Underneath the floorboards of the engine room were rolled-up marine charts for places like the Mediterranean, Florida and Lebanon, a major player in global hash production in the 1980s.
"This is a dope smuggling ship and they're hiding the charts," Gordon realized.
He later interviewed U.S., Canadian and British police to piece together Adeline-C's origins for some stories in the Chronicle-Herald.
Retrofitted to smuggle drugs

Other features advantageous for drug smuggling that had been retrofitted on the 1963 trawler were high-capacity fuel tanks and winches, elevators and cranes that made it easier for the mother ship to carry out hefty cargo transfers to smaller ships at sea. The smaller vessels then smuggled the drugs into ports along the East Coast, targeting the U.S. and possibly Canada.
With its countless isolated bays and inlets, Nova Scotia has long been a popular destination for smugglers, be it rum or drugs.

items: How a $500M Cape Breton drug bust helped inspire the film Little Lorraine

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the Halifax sheriff's department told the Toronto Star in 1982 he was perplexed by the situation.
"She has a 1,000-horse diesel [engine] aboard and that would drive her right smart through anything," he said. "No one in his right mind would walk away from something like that."
But abandoning a valuable ship was just a minor business expense for the people who owned the Adeline-C.
"What they were making was so much more," said Gordon.

The Federal Court ordered that the Adeline-C be sold in late 1982, with the sale planned for January 1983, but the Toronto Star reported another round of bids might take place because the highest original bid was $76,000 "from a bargain-hunting local fisherman."

An article in the Sept. 14, 1986, Chicago Tribune included a photo of Robert Christopher (Chris) Murray, the alleged mastermind behind the drug operation. He was never tried for his alleged role in the drug ring because he fled. (www.newspapers.com)
Ultimately, its buyer was a Dutch man named Erik van Veenen. At that point in his life, he was living in Alaska, running a trading post and a hunting business.
After a ship purchase in Nova Scotia fell through, a lawyer involved with the failed transaction tipped him off about the Adeline-C.
After seeing the ship and the equipment on it, he figured it was worth a million dollars.
"So I fell in love with the boat and I bought it and I've regretted it ever since," said van Veenen, now 82 and living in Germany.
He believes he paid around $100,000 US for it.
Two people walk hand in hand on April 8, 2020, in Newport, R.I. The drug scheme was based out of the small coastal city. (Steven Senne/AP)
One day as he worked to get the ship ready to go back to Alaska, he pulled up the floorboards in the engine room, much like Gordon had done.

"I came across this big, blue logbook, all handwritten with the complete description of the journey of the boat: Amsterdam to Gibraltar to Cairo through the Suez Canal to Djibouti and then on past Singapore," said van Veenen.
Iran-Contra affair?

He believes the ship wasn't just into drug running, but was used for transporting weapons as part of the Iran-Contra affair, in which the U.S. made a deal to secretly sell weapons to Iran in exchange for the release of hostages being held by the Iranian-backed group Hezbollah in Lebanon.
While conducting interviews and reading through court documents and dozens of newspaper articles to research this story, the reporter did not come across any references to the Iran-Contra affair.
The Gesmer I, formerly the Adeline-C, is shown in St. John's Harbour in 1992. (Capt. Harry Stone/Maritime History Archive)

When van Veenen left Halifax, his plan was to sail the ship south along the Atlantic coastline, cross through the Panama Canal and then head north to Alaska, but financial troubles killed the plans. The Adeline-C was costly to run and a sale of his trading post soured, leaving him financially squeezed.
At some point, he'd changed the name of the ship to Thackeray C, in honour of his then wife.
Van Veenen said he posted the trawler for sale in a boating magazine, and the next buyer was based in Quebec.
By October 1984, the Adeline-C — now operating as the Thackeray C — was briefly accused of being the mother ship in a high-seas transfer of arms destined for use by the Irish Republican Army.

While an unidentified spokesperson for the Irish national police made that assertion to Gordon, a followup story a day later quoted a Canadian customs official who said the ship had been in Gaspé, Que., since July of that year.
FBI, IRS investigation

The year 1984 also marked the year that a task force involving the FBI, the Internal Revenue Service and the Drug Enforcement Administration started questioning suspects in Rhode Island about the drug operation, according to a 1988 Providence Journal article.

The investigation was aided by records obtained by police in Guernsey, an island in the English Channel, which contained "almost a diary of the whole operation," detailing names, dates, costs and expected profits, the newspaper reported.
The alleged mastermind behind the fraud was a Rhode Island resident named Robert Christopher (Chris) Murray.
How the money behind the drug operation was obtained

Accounts vary, but he obtained at least $10 million US in loans from the Guernsey branch of the First National Bank of Chicago. Murray used yachts owned by people well known "among the yachting fraternity in Rhode Island" as collateral, the Chicago Tribune reported in 1986.
The pitch was that the money would be used to distribute mortgages to clients who would buy and refit luxury yachts.

However, the Chicago Tribune reported that the notary public who vouched for the yacht owners and notarized financial statements did not exist, according to the federal government. Rather, it was believed the signatures belonged to Murray. The people who owned the supposed assets were fictitious.
In reality, the money was for the drug operation and the only boats purchased would be four mother ships in Holland, of which one never left the shipyard.
Of the three vessels that took part in the scheme, the Adeline-C was dubbed "the most mysterious ship of all," according to a 1984 Providence Journal article.
Journalist Rob Gordon, shown in a 2007 CBC News report, learned about the Adeline-C while working as a newspaper reporter in 1981. (CBC)

Before it was purchased for the drug operation, it was known as the Hilda H. It was purchased in Holland for 423,370 Swiss francs — about $219,000 US — on April 13, 1981. It then underwent some retrofitting to have state-of-the-art equipment installed that would prove beneficial in running drugs.

Newspaper accounts covering the drug operation predominantly focus on the roles of the other ships — the Caroline C and the Sea Scout — as the ports they visited were well documented and some of their smuggling was thwarted by authorities.
It's unclear where the Adeline-C picked up its drugs, with Lebanon and Thailand listed in varying newspaper accounts.
How the Adeline-C ended up in Halifax
But once it returned to North America, the Adeline-C met up at Georges Bank off Nova Scotia to unload roughly 12,000 pounds of marijuana, according to a 1986 Chicago Tribune article.
While half was transferred to one ship, the newspaper said the remainder of the drugs had to be dumped overboard when another ship, the Side Show, didn't show up.
Aerial view of Providence, R.I., on Aug. 1, 2019. Some of the court cases related to the drug ring were held here. (Eva Claire Hambach/AFP via Getty Images)

When the Adeline-C arrived in Halifax on Halloween 1981, the only cargo it contained was a rifle, a handgun and a load of teak that had been used to disguise the drugs, according to one of Gordon's stories.

In Rhode Island, about 18 people ended up indicted for their role in Murray's drug operation, and most were convicted, with the cases largely tried before the U.S. District Court in Providence, Rhode Island's capital, the Providence Journal-Bulletin reported.
As for the alleged mastermind, he was never brought before the courts because he couldn't be located.
Murray was wanted in Illinois, North Carolina and Rhode Island for bank fraud, drug smuggling and income tax evasion, according to a 1988 Providence Journal article.
His last known address was in Guadeloupe in the Caribbean, but he later fled to Spain and lived under an assumed name, the newspaper reported.
This Nov. 20, 2011, photo shows the West Indies island of Guadeloupe. Chris Murray's last known address was on this island. (Jean Michel Andre/AFP via Getty Images)
But Murray didn't live a quiet life. He rented a Spanish villa and drove three cars, including a Porsche.
It was in a car, a white Ford, where Murray's life came to an end in 1987. He'd been shot three times and his burning vehicle was found in a grove of eucalyptus trees.
Fingerprints taken from the body and processed by an FBI lab in Washington later confirmed his identity, the Providence Journal reported.
People sunbathe on the beach of Torremolinos, Spain, on July 20, 2015. It was in this community where Chris Murray was found slain in 1987. (Jorge Guerrero/AFP via Getty Images)
The Adeline-C is still alive, but it goes by the name of Gesmer I, according to various ship tracking websites. At the time of writing, it was in Dominica in the Caribbean.
Looking back on the Adeline-C's time in Halifax, Gordon thinks about other ships.
"Back around that time, there was an enormous amount of drug smuggling ... tons and tons of dope from all sorts of directions was arriving here," he said.
"And that ship, because it was abandoned, because it was downtown Halifax, it sort of stuck out. But it certainly wouldn't have been the only ship that did that."

articles.title: Quiboloy counsel says Cendaña went beyond 'permitted commentary'
articles.summary: The counsel of detained preacher Apollo Quiboloy thumbed down Akbayan party-list Representative Percival "Perci" Cendaña free speech defense against the libel and cyber libel complaint that the…

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 4:34pm

The counsel of detained preacher Apollo Quiboloy thumbed down Akbayan party-list Representative Percival "Perci" Cendaña free speech defense against the libel and cyber libel complaint that the religious leader filed against the lawmaker.
Quiboloy, through his legal counsel Ferdinand Topacio, filed the complaint against Cendaña, Mamamayang Liberal party-list Representative Leila de Lima, and Senator Risa Hontiveros last September.
"The statements of Mr. Cendaña went beyond the bounds of permitted commentary, and clearly crossed the line into criminal defamation," Topacio said.
"We will prove malice in view of a long history of ill-will against Pastor Quiboloy, and a long-running intention to malign his good name," he added.
Topacio accused Cendaña of singling out Quiboloy for a selfish political agenda.
On Friday, Cendaña filed his counter-affidavit regarding the libel and cyber libel complaint that Quiboloy's camp filed against him.
The complaint stemmed from a radio interview, wherein Cendaña supposedly issued statements such as:
"Nakita naman natin kung papaano isa-isa 'yung mga witnesses tinatakot at hinaharass nila para bumaligtad, 'no? At kahit 'yung mga biktima, tinakot at hinarass nila para hindi ituloy ang laban."
(We have seen how witnesses were threatened and harassed to change their statements. Even the victims were threatened and harassed to discourage them from pursuing their cases.)

The lawmaker issued the comments in relation to the various charges that the pastor was facing, including qualified human trafficking, child abuse, and sex trafficking in both the United States and the Philippines.
Washington has formally sought to extradite Quiboloy from the Philippines to face justice in the US.
In his affidavit, Cendaña cited free speech enshrined in Article III, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution.

"The complainant has not established the elements necessary to bring my statements outside the protection afforded to good faith public commentary under the Constitution and applicable jurisprudence," Cendaña said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: The races that will decide control of the US Senate
articles.summary: Democrats are now competitive in states Donald Trump won handily in 2024, even as Republicans seek to capture Democratic-held seats of their own

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, DC, USA – Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats in November’s midterm elections to wrest control of the US Senate from Republicans, with voter discontent over President Donald Trump, the Iran war and rising prices putting races in once-solidly Republican states into play.

Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, and a Democratic takeover looked unlikely at the start of the year. But Democrats are now competitive in states Trump won handily in 2024, even as Republicans seek to capture Democratic-held seats of their own.
Here are the races that could determine control of the Senate:
Alaska
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is up for reelection against Democratic former US Representative Mary Peltola and an outsider who shares Sullivan’s name.

Alaska allows voters to rank their top picks rather than choosing a single candidate. Voters will have four choices, including Sullivan, Peltola, and the other Dan Sullivan, a candidate Republicans have called a decoy in what they believe is a Democratic effort to confuse voters.
Trump’s midterm travel this month included a stop in Alaska.

Peltola has outraised Sullivan through October, $33 million to nearly $14 million. But Sullivan reported having more campaign cash, $5.1 million to Peltola’s $3.2 million, and Republicans have outspent Democrats, $42 million to $38 million.
Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024, but recent opinion polls show Peltola narrowly leading Sullivan.
Iowa
Trump’s unpopularity, tariffs and the Iran war have put Republicans on defense in Iowa, where Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

Republican US Senator Joni Ernst’s decision not to seek reelection has made this an open-seat contest between Republican US Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist.

Hinson has called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war and said Iowans should not have to pay higher fuel or grocery prices as a result of it. However, she has repeatedly voted against resolutions in Congress calling for an end to the war.
Turek has outraised Hinson, $20 million to $14 million. But Hinson reported $3 million more cash on hand through September, and Republicans have outspent Democrats, $81 million to $70 million.
Recent polls show Hinson with a narrow lead.
Kansas

The political environment has shifted in favor of Democrats so much that Kansas is now in play. Republicans have diverted resources from North Carolina to shore up US Senator Roger Marshall, who in recent weeks has condemned the activity of Immigration and Customs Enforcement in his state.

Trump won Kansas by 16 points in 2024, but the state has twice elected Democratic Governor Laura Kelly. And Republican leaders have acknowledged the race is competitive and closer than they would like it to be.

Marshall’s opponent is Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of a Methodist megachurch. Hamilton has outraised Marshall, $14 million to $6 million, and reported more cash on hand, $3.2 million to $922,000, through September.
In a reversal of the usual pattern, Democratic groups have outspent Republicans in Kansas, $28 million to $22 million.
The last time Kansas voters elected a Democrat to the US Senate was 1932. Most recent polls show Hamilton leading narrowly.
Maine
Democrats’ top pickup opportunity to begin the cycle was in Maine, the lone state where a Republican incumbent is up for reelection in a state Trump lost in 2024.
Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic opponent, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, were both joined on the campaign trail by big-name supporters last week.

Collins stumped with former US Senator Joe Manchin, a West Virginia independent who left the Democratic Party in 2024, while Jackson held a town hall with US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

Manchin’s joint appearance with Collins came after the senator distanced herself from Trump at a debate earlier this month, when Collins — who voted to convict Trump after he was impeached following the January 6, 2021, assault on the US Capitol — acknowledged that she isn’t the president’s favorite senator and said he wouldn’t be coming to Maine.

Democrats say Collins only votes against Trump when it doesn’t matter — such as when she voted against a sweeping tax-cut package last year after backing it in a procedural vote. Democrats also hope voters will hold her accountable for helping confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the US Supreme Court, which led to the overturning of a federal right to abortion.

Democrats, however, have their own drama. The party’s original nominee, progressive oysterman Graham Platner, was pressured into withdrawing following sexual assault allegations, forcing the state party to scramble for a new candidate. Platner denied the allegations.

Jackson, another progressive, emerged as Platner’s replacement, but he has drawn criticism for his treatment of women. He has said publicly he doesn’t regret telling Collins to “shut up” at a recent debate. Jackson’s female allies publicly defended his character and legislative record last week, when the Maine Women’s Lobby endorsed him over Collins.

Jackson has outraised Collins by more than $1.6 million despite not entering the race until July. But Collins has a $1.1 million advantage in cash on hand as of mid-October. Republican groups have outspent Democrats, $76 million to $40 million.
Recent polls show Jackson with a narrow lead or tied.
North Carolina
Republicans appear to have conceded North Carolina, where even Trump has suggested the Democrat will win.
At a campaign rally last week in Greenville, Trump told supporters it was “crazy” that former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, was going to be their next senator.
Trump won North Carolina by 3 points in 2024, but Republican Senator Thom Tillis’ retirement made this year’s Senate race an open contest.

Trump recruited former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley to succeed Tillis, but the ex-party official has been unable to compete with Cooper’s fundraising, and Republican allies who invested heavily in holding North Carolina have begun shifting their focus to other states.
Cooper has raised $50 million and has $9 million in the bank. Whatley has raised $14 million and has just $900,000 on hand through mid-October.
Recent polls have Cooper leading by double digits.
Ohio
Democrat Sherrod Brown is seeking to return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024, and working-class frustration with the Iran war and rising prices may be giving him a tailwind.

This time, Brown faces US Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to replace US Vice President JD Vance when Vance left the Senate for the White House. The winner of the special election will be on the ballot again in 2028 for a full six-year term.

The Ohio race has become one of the most expensive Senate contests in the nation. Republican and Democratic outside groups have each spent nine figures on the race, with Republicans investing $232 million and Democrats pouring in $118 million.

Brown has more than tripled Husted’s fundraising through October 14, bringing in $68 million to Husted’s nearly $20 million. Both campaigns reported having a little more than $4 million to spend as of mid-October.
Recent polls show Brown leading by 3 to 5 points.
Texas
No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994. James Talarico, a state representative, could break the streak.
Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the big, conservative-leaning state that has dashed Democratic hopes repeatedly in recent years.

Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024. Yet Republican outside groups have already spent $300 million to hold the seat after runoff voters nominated the scandal-plagued Paxton over incumbent Republican US Senator John Cornyn. Trump endorsed Paxton even though Cornyn was widely believed to have an easier path to victory.
Leaked audio has exposed daylight between Trump and Paxton, who privately told donors that the president’s midterm convention hurt his campaign.

Democratic groups have spent $76 million on this race. But Talarico’s campaign has outraised Paxton’s by $110 million and reported $9.6 million more in its campaign coffers as of September 30. Paxton’s donors include billionaire Elon Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X, ​and other businesses there. Musk has given $158 million to a Republican super PAC to invest in Paxton’s race.
Recent polls show Talarico narrowly leading or tied.
Georgia

Georgia was one of two key pickup opportunities for Republicans at the beginning of the election cycle, as Trump won the state by 2 percentage points in 2024. But Republican US Representative Mike Collins has struggled to gain traction against Democratic US Senator Jon Ossoff, a potential 2028 presidential candidate.
Ossoff has outraised Collins by nearly $126 million through October 14 and began mid-October with $15.1 million in his war chest compared to Collins’ $1.1 million.
Polls have consistently shown Ossoff leading, and Democrats narrowly lead Republicans in outside spending, $19 million to $17.9 million.
Michigan

Republicans are more hopeful about flipping an open seat in Michigan, especially after the Democratic establishment didn’t get its pick. Progressive outsider Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated moderate US Representative Haley Stevens during the primary, putting him on a collision course with Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative, in what could be the tightest race for a Democratic-held Senate seat this year.
Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned in Michigan over the weekend.

A pro-Israel super PAC has spent at least $493,000 against El-Sayed, a follow-up to its $30 million effort to stop him from winning the Democratic nomination. The super PAC could spend as much as $9 million in the general election.
El-Sayed’s allies have also stepped up, with US Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Ocasio-Cortez each putting $1 million behind his campaign.
El-Sayed has raised $45 million through September, more than double Rogers’ nearly $21 million. But Rogers began October with more on hand, $6.5 million to $3.8 million.
Republicans have poured $136 million into the Senate race in Michigan, where Democrats have spent more than $70 million.
Most recent polls show El-Sayed with a narrow lead.
New Hampshire
Democrats are defending another open seat in New Hampshire, though this is a state then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris won by nearly 3 points in 2024.
Democratic US Representative Chris Pappas is running against former US Senator John Sununu, who was ousted by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. Shaheen is retiring.

Sununu benefits from a famous last name. His brother Chris was governor until last year, and his father — also named John — was a governor and White House chief of staff for President George H.W. Bush.
Pappas has raised four times as much as Sununu, $24 million to $6 million. Pappas has a modest $200,000 cash advantage, but Republicans have spent $37 million in the race to Democrats’ $20 million.
Pappas has maintained a consistent polling lead of 5 to 8 points in recent surveys. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Cocaine smuggler could avoid prison as judge fears incarceration would orphan 7-year-old son
articles.summary: A Toronto judge is weighing whether to send a single father to prison for importing cocaine into Newfoundland and Labrador during the pandemic, or find an alternate sentence that could "break the…

image.caption: An Ontario judge will soon decide whether or not to send a single father to prison for shipping cocaine to Newfoundland during the pandemic. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

A Toronto judge is weighing whether to send a single father to prison for importing cocaine into Newfoundland and Labrador during the pandemic, or find an alternate sentence that could "break the cycle" for his seven-year-old boy.
Justice Louis Strezos pondering measures to 'break the cycle'
There is no denying Steven Armstrong played a pivotal role in a pandemic-era scheme to sneak $1 million worth of cocaine into Newfoundland and Labrador.

The Newmarket, Ont., man's co-conspirators were caught red-handed by the Mounties with 3.4 kilograms stashed in the airbag compartment of a Honda Ridgeline pickup truck. Armstrong even pleaded guilty.
But is it worth sending a single father to prison if it means his seven-year-old son will become a ward of the state?
That's the question now being pondered by Justice Louis Strezos of the Ontario Court of Justice.

"Is there not a concern that Jackson may repeat the sins of his father if I make him an orphan?" Strezos asked during a sentencing hearing on Thursday, in which he called the lawyers back to the courtroom to ask more questions before making a decision.
The Crown and defence are miles apart in their submissions to the court.
Defence lawyer Adam Boni is asking for a conditional sentence order of less than two years — essentially house arrest.

Crown prosecutor Christopher Kalantzsis was asking for a prison sentence of up to seven years, but reduced his request to four to five years on Thursday after learning of the sentences for Armstrong's co-conspirators in Newfoundland.
Dion Wilson Lee Rodgers and Edmond Dorman Pickett pleaded not guilty, but were convicted by a jury of their peers after a trial in Gander, N.L.
Rodgers was sentenced to 39 months, while Pickett received a 34-month sentence.
The court in Newfoundland heard the investigation began in 2018 after police noticed Armstrong was making frequent, short trips to the island through the Marine Atlantic ferry system.
A court case in central Newfoundland is shining a light on how drugs travelled into the province from Ontario in 2020 through the Marine Atlantic ferry system. (Brittany Wentzell/CBC)

Armstrong was stopped during one of those visits in 2019, but police failed to find any drugs in his vehicle. Investigators continued tracking Armstrong into 2020, when they learned he planned to transport a pickup truck to Newfoundland. The province went into lockdown in March due to the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving Armstrong unable to gain entry.

In September 2020, police learned Armstrong had left Ontario in the truck and was driving towards the ferry terminal in Nova Scotia. At the same time, police observed Rodgers and his stepfather drive onto the ferry on the other side of the crossing in Newfoundland.
Rodgers's stepfather got in the Honda Ridgeline when they got to the other side, and headed back to Newfoundland, where he was stopped by police.

In a surprising twist, a search of the vehicle turned up no drugs. Officers later intercepted a message between Rodgers and Armstrong, which led them to look inside the airbag compartment on the passenger side. There, they found 3.4 kilograms of cocaine in a customized module with a hydraulic release system.
Judge voices concern for child
The court in Ontario heard Steven Armstrong has a lengthy criminal record, with his last convictions resulting in federal time in 2011.
Kalantzsis referred to Armstrong as a "recidivist drug offender," while Boni argued his record is dated and less relevant.
Armstrong never knew his father, the court heard, and grew up in the child welfare system.
Boni pointed out that Armstrong hasn't reoffended in the five years he's been on bail conditions for his most recent charges, and said his son has had a major impact on his life choices.

"In a twist of cruel fate the young boy's challenges and the nature of the care he requires and the fact that Mr. Armstrong is the only person who can deliver it has actually commenced the process of rehabilitation in the intervening period," Boni said. "The connection between this boy and his father is not only relevant from the collateral consequence on the boy, but is also relevant to the rehabilitation of this offender in a marked way."

Kalantzsis argued the sentence shouldn't be guided solely by Armstrong's prospects for rehabilitation, but by a need to find a sentence that matches the gravity of the offence and the moral blameworthiness of the offender.
"I don't make any submission that incarcerating Mr. Armstrong is not going to bad for the child," Kalantzsis said. "There is no doubt about that."

"But let me narrow that down a bit more," Strezos said. "The undisputed record before me is that this child will become an orphan and will go to group homes, right? That's the record ... I'm left in the situation where I have a child who is now eight? Seven? Who will go to a group home and potentially be subject to the very forces and dynamics that led to Mr. Armstrong's criminality."
Strezos said there is an avenue available to him, through a sentence like house arrest, that could "break that cycle ... and it's on my mind."
Strezos will render his decision on Nov. 12.

Ryan Cooke is a justice affairs reporter based in St. John's. He can be reached at ryan.cooke@cbc.ca.

articles.title: ‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifies
articles.summary:
Mouria coffeehouse unable to renew lease in Exarchia, known for leftwing solidarity, resistance and radicalism

It has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and…

blocks.text: It has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44 years, Christos Vanas, the proprietor of Mouria, has let them all in.

Every day at 7am, the taciturn former waiter has been the first man to step inside the historic cafe in Exarchia, the heart of leftwing Athens. It is a ritual he has kept punctiliously, opening up the famous gathering place before he himself has had his first coffee.

blocks.caption: Christos Vanas and his daughter Areti will close Mouria on Sunday.

blocks.text: “Only Saturdays are different,” says his daughter Areti, drawing on a Karelia, the aromatic Greek cigarette that, like Mouria, has been around for more than a century. “By 5am, he is here serving tsipouro and other [alcoholic] spirits to warm up the stallholders of the street market outside.”

But this weekend will be Vanas’s last. After a send-off expected to last into the small hours, the cafe’s large, iron-framed doors will shut forever on Sunday when patrons walk out of the mosaic-floored institution. It will be the closing act in a drama that began with the expiry of the premises’ lease last summer.

blocks.caption: ‘It will be as if a friend died,’ says Nontas Papayiannis, a retired lawyer who has visited Mouria almost every day for 20 years.  Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The Guardian

blocks.text: “It will be as if a friend died,” sighs Nontas Papayannis, a retired barrister who has frequented the cafe for the past 20 years. “Another change to Exarchia, but also another loss in a Greece that is dying before our eyes.”

Born and bred in the neighbourhood long viewed as the nerve centre of Athens’ counterculture scene, the blue-eyed septuagenarian has also kept to a regime, rocking up at his favourite watering hole “at least four times a week” within an hour of the clock striking noon.

blocks.caption: ‘A visit here is the route to relaxation,’ said Stelios Goutis, a retired actor.  Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The Guardian

blocks.text: Stelios Goutis, 83, is an actor who trod the boards for more than six decades before his fame broadened playing Papa Triantafyllos, a priest with a penchant for a tipple or two in the TV series Hara’s Cafe. He waxes lyrical about“the calming effect” of traditional eateries that have had such an outsized role in the lives of Greeks.

“A visit here is the route to relaxation,” Goutis says with thespian flair at one of Mouria’s marble-topped tables. “You stop by after work. You down a tsipouro or two, you meet friends you may or may not have arranged to meet, and all the pressures of daily life slip away. It’s a form of psychotherapy. When it goes, we’ll look back at it as a memory of good times even if it is a loss, too.”

Both men were among the 7,500 signatories of an online campaign that urged the Greek culture ministry to have the cafe declared a protected heritage site when the building’s owners announced they would not be renewing its tenancy in an area fast undergoing gentrification. The culture ministry failed to intervene.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: ‘So much has changed’ in Exarchia, said Areti. ‘You could be anywhere.’ Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The Guardian

blocks.text: Few districts in downtown Athens are more redolent of resistance, leftwing solidarity, radicalism and anarchist foment than Exarchia. Its spirit of anti-authoritarianism dates back to the uprising at the nearby Athens Polytechnic, an event that led to the death of dozens of students but is credited with the collapse of rightwing military rule in 1974, barely 35 years after the nation’s bitter civil war.

But with tourist numbers in the Greek capital more than doubling over the last decade, the neighbourhood of narrow, graffiti-daubed streets has also been discovered by investors, catering to the tastes and needs of foreign visitors.

“We were like the last fortress here,” says Areti, dressed in a black leather jacket and Dr Martens boots, the garb favoured by the area’s more youthful residents. “We didn’t change our menu, we didn’t raise our prices or serve Aperol spritzes and cafe lattes. It’s about nostalgia and we’ll leave with our heads held high.”

For Greeks raised in Exarchia, it was an unnerving experience to walk streets that were no longer recognisable, she lamented. “So much has changed. Everywhere you look there are new shops with signs in English and buildings turned into suites and short-term rentals. You could be anywhere.”

For many, the last straw had come when travel platforms began advertising tours of the hangouts in Exarchia patronised by hardened leftists. “There have been groups outside the cafe,” says Areti, her eyes firmly focused on her footwear. “What to say?”

Mouria is not alone. Its closure is emblematic of the decline of traditional coffee houses across Greece, even if the proliferation of third-wave and Italian-style cafes in more recent years has earned the country the reputation of having “a cafe economy”.

blocks.caption: ‘We were like the last fortress here,’ Areti said. Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The Guardian

blocks.text: In villages far and wide, kafeneia once considered the life and soul of communities are vanishing, turbocharging depopulation.

But in Exarchia, among local people so fervently opposed to corporate culture, the end of the landmark coffeeshop on the corner of Charilaou Trikoupi and Kallidromiou streets is also part of a concerted effort to alter the neighbourhood’s traditional leftwing identity. Anger has similarly mounted over the construction of a metro station in Exarchia’s main square, championed by the centre-right government as a way of cleaning up a district that many conservatives regard as an affront to their own ideology. The public work, which has resulted in increased policing, has deprived residents of their one open space to gather.

“Exarchia is perhaps the only neighbourhood in Athens where the leftwing concept of the ‘revanchist city’ is applicable,” notes Nicos Souliotis, a sociologist at the National Centre for Social Research. “State policies are clearly aimed at imposing social discipline and control. The activism we have seen around Mouria is about defending the neighbourhood’s identity and established way of life.”

blocks.caption: Mouria’s closure is emblematic of the decline of traditional coffee houses across Greece. Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The Guardian

blocks.text: For Maria Tsampra, another longtime veteran of the cafe and a former employee of the defunct leftwing daily newspaper Eleftherotypia, the sociologist is spot on.

Enjoying what will be one of her last platters of mezedes at Mouria, she says the cafe’s closure is as much about “erasing memory” – because that, she adds, is also part of the neighbourhood’s “all for profit” transformation – as it is shutting down a leftwing stronghold in the heart of Athens.

“There’s this attempt at revisionism, of controlling us through the rewriting of history,” Tsampra says before breaking into a smile: “It won’t work. In Mouria we found a haven and we won’t be forgetting it anytime soon.”
