articles.title: Responsible or panicked? Meet the people around the world already preparing for crisis
articles.summary: Filter straws to a disposable toilet - people in the US, Japan, Sweden and Netherlands on what's in their emergency stashes.

blocks.text: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement.
"It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.

A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.

Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.

His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.

Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.
In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.
Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".
Ayumi T, who lives in Tokyo, has kept an emergency bag for years in case of events like earthquakes, typhoons and extreme heat.
But after an earthquake in 2024 killed hundreds of people and caused widespread damage to Japan's Noto Peninsula, Ayumi stocked up even more.
Tokyo's government has a 68-page disaster prevention guide, external, which details what to keep in an emergency kit and what to do in certain emergency situations.

In her emergency rucksack - kept in her wardrobe - Ayumi keeps clothes, towels, menstrual products, disposable chopsticks, sticky notes, disposable masks and a disposable toilet, like those used by hikers and campers.
"A lot of it is old stuff I don't use anymore," Ayumi, 27, who works at a university, says.
Every new year, her family check their kits and update them if necessary, replacing out-of-date food, for example.
Over the past five years, "it's been on my mind, 'what happens in case of emergency?'", Nicole Bonds says.
The leadership coach in Atlanta, puts this down to noticing "significantly more and more" severe weather patterns and storms around the world and a lack of preparedness.
Her motto is "don't panic, be prepared", she says.
As well as a large selection of cleaning and hygiene products, Nicole, 48, has bought batteries, a power bank, first-aid supplies, rechargeable fans, blankets and sleeping bags.
To keep it affordable she picks up a small amount of supplies "here and there" to gradually build up her stock. She keeps some of the items under her bed, in packing bags and in her kitchen cabinets.
Where Michael Stuut lives in the Netherlands is below sea level. He says he worries about extreme weather but also possible war.
The 39-year-old, who lives in Hoorn with his wife and five-year-old son, started preparing his kit a few years ago.
Michael keeps a healthy stash of power equipment as well as food - including a Starlink Mini, a small and lightweight satellite device for internet access.
He keeps supplies in his attic and a crawl space under the house - here lies about 120 litres of water, cash, a first-aid kit and a generator.
Earlier this year, Michael created an app to log his food supplies and when they might expire.
"Being prepared isn't about panic," he says. "It's about being the calm one when the lights go out."
In late 2025, Dutch authorities launched a campaign that instructed households to have 72 hours' worth of supplies, much like UK authorities have just done.

At the beginning of his prepping journey, Michael's wife didn't see the need, but he says she now understands the importance. They've told their five-year-old the supplies are simply for when they don't want to go to the shop, adding they "don't want to burden him".

Michael is sceptical of the three-day advice - also recommended by the UK - but says: "Every household that has a few basic things at home makes it easier for the emergency services to help the people who need it most."
Additional reporting by Hanae Takahashi and Richard Frost

articles.title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
articles.summary: Countries have been trying to get a global agreement to halt nature decline back on track.

blocks.text: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.
The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.
Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.
"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.
Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.
That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.
They agreed that action was urgent.
The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.
But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.
As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.
"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.
"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.

This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."
But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".
Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland.
Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.

items: Bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF

blocks.text: Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.
In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.

But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , external
At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.

Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment.
"A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."
Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice.
"So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."

A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually - at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.
Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged.

"When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."
One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature.
But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process.
"The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency.

Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding.

"This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

articles.title: Men can also be victims of sexual violence — Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has upheld the conviction of a woman for statutory acts of lasciviousness after she sexually abused her 11-year-old nephew, stressing that men can also be victims of sexual violence.

blocks.text: Content warning: This article discusses child sexual abuse, sexual violence and trauma, including suicidal thoughts.

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has upheld the conviction of a woman for statutory acts of lasciviousness after she sexually abused her 11-year-old nephew, stressing that men can also be victims of sexual violence.
In a decision penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the SC said victims should not be expected to react in a particular way after an incident of sexual abuse.

“Sexual violence devastates equally, regardless of gender. However, people may vary in their reactions and the way they cope with distressing situations,” the decision read, which was released to the public on Friday, October 30.
“Thus, the fact that a person's reaction to an incident is different from what is deemed ‘standard,’ does not diminish the credibility of their claims,” it added.
What happened

The case stemmed from an incident on Sept. 7, 2018, when the accused, the boy's paternal aunt, allegedly woke him (AAA280727) in the middle of the night and ordered him to remove his clothes and lie on the bed.
She then put a condom on his penis, got on top of him and inserted his penis into her vagina. The incident lasted about 10 minutes.
The accused allegedly warned the boy not to tell anyone, threatening to accuse him of rape if he did.
The boy said he initially did not resist because he was curious about what would happen.

On Feb. 16, 2019, the boy's maternal uncle confronted him about a group chat discussing his alleged experience with a college girl. The boy then told his uncle about what happened between him and the accused.

A doctor then conducted a psychological debriefing and provided supportive psychotherapy to the boy. He was later diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder after experiencing anxiety, depression, flashbacks, nightmares and suicidal thoughts.

The accused denied the allegations and argued that the boy's behavior showed that he had consented to or enjoyed the incident. She also questioned his credibility, pointing to his initial lack of resistance and his alleged reactions during the incident.

The accused's defense also presented the testimonies of her sister, mother and brother. She claimed that she had slept in another room with her siblings on the night of the incident, while the boy slept with his cousin, grandmother and father. Her sister and mother corroborated her account.
Her brother, who was also the boy's father, claimed that the case was filed against her because of a custody dispute between him and his estranged wife.
RTC, CA rulings

In a Dec. 2, 2022 decision, the Regional Trial Court (RTC) in Manila found the accused guilty beyond reasonable doubt of acts of lasciviousness in relation to Section 5(b) of Republic Act No. 7610, or the Special Protection of Children Against Child Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act.
The RTC sentenced her to 12 years and one day of reclusion temporal, as minimum, to 14 years, eight months and one day of reclusion temporal, as maximum.
It also ordered her to pay the boy P50,000 in civil indemnity, P50,000 in moral damages and P50,000 in exemplary damages.

The accused appealed the ruling, but the Court of Appeals (CA) denied her appeal in an Aug. 30, 2024 decision. It upheld her conviction but increased the maximum prison term to 16 years, five months and nine days of reclusion temporal.
The CA denied her motion for reconsideration on April 29, 2025. The accused then brought the case before the Supreme Court.
SC on male victims of sexual violence
The SC rejected the accused's arguments questioning the boy's credibility, including her claim that his behavior indicated that he enjoyed the incident.
The high court said victims should not be expected to resist or respond in a particular way when they are intimidated or under emotional stress.
“Victims of rape or sexual abuse should not be burdened to resist or to have a standard reaction when intimidated and under emotional stress,” the high court said.
“Thus, AAA280727's reaction, which differs from what is deemed to be normal, does not invalidate his claims.”
The high court also discussed how the country's rape laws have historically treated sexual violence involving male victims.

It noted that, under the wording of the law before Republic Act No. 11648, rape through sexual intercourse was defined as a man having carnal knowledge of a woman. This left a gap in cases where a woman forced a man to have sexual intercourse with her by causing the insertion of his penis into her vagina.

The SC said that even more recent rulings continued to interpret rape in the context of male penile insertion rather than broadly covering intercourse involving a penis and a vagina, regardless of who initiates it.
“These views on rape are not only misogynistic, they also disenfranchise male victims who have less redress in law, but are inflicted with the same trauma,” the high court said.
“Further, the lack of recognition that males can be victims also impairs their ability to recognize that they have been violated in the first place,” it added.
It noted that while the law must recognize the historical injustice suffered by women, its interpretation must also protect victims regardless of gender.
“When laws are not gender-neutral, male victims suffer twice: once at the hands of their abuser and second through the judicial system,” the SC said.
The high court also described rape as an issue of power and an imposition of dominance that violates another person's bodily autonomy.
“In this case, petitioner used her age and moral ascendancy to coerce a then 11-year-old AAA280727 into satisfying her lewd intentions,” it said.
Woman can be held liable for rape under amended law

In a separate concurring opinion, Associate Justice Jhosep Lopez said the acts committed by the accused would constitute rape under Article 266-A(1) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA No. 11648.
“These acts are constitutive of rape under Republic Act No. 11648,” Lopez said.
He explained that the amendment expanded the definition of rape through sexual intercourse to cover any person who has carnal knowledge of another person, regardless of gender.
“With the advent of Republic Act No. 11648, rape through sexual intercourse can be consummated by any person having carnal knowledge with anyone, regardless of gender,” Lopez said.

“Thus, a woman can be held liable of rape through sexual intercourse for having a carnal knowledge with a man, without the latter's consent, under Article 266-A(1) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended.”
However, Lopez pointed out that the incident happened in 2018, before RA No. 11648 took effect in 2022.

He said the amendment could not be applied retroactively to the accused because doing so would result in a heavier penalty, which would not be favorable to her under Article 22 of the Revised Penal Code.
“However, the said acts were committed in 2018 before the effectivity of Republic Act No. 11648,” he said.

“Nonetheless, as Republic Act No. 11648 still does not apply to the present case. XXX280727 must be held liable for the crime of statutory acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code.”
Penalty
The SC held the accused liable for statutory acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code.
It sentenced her to imprisonment ranging from nine years, four months and one day of prision mayor, as minimum, to 16 years, five months and nine days of reclusion temporal, as maximum.

The high court also ordered her to pay the victim P150,000 in civil indemnity, P50,000 in moral damages and P50,000 in exemplary damages, with 6% annual interest from the finality of the decision until full payment.

articles.title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
articles.summary:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott

The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign…

blocks.text: The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.

European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.

During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in front of Lavrov and said Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.

A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”

The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.

Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.

Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.

But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

articles.title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
articles.summary: From Alaska to Texas, candidates with an eye on Congress are using their personal style to stand out.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByNardine Saad
US reporter
As Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.
In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal.
"Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.
From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.
Dressing like their state
Some candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.
The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022.
She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.

Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from".
"Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.
Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gluesenkamp Perez chooses a workwear-inspired wardrobe

blocks.text: Image source, BBC News
Gluesenkamp Perez chooses a workwear-inspired wardrobe
Democratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.
She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.
During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.
The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mary Peltola wore the traditional footwear of the Yup'ik people when she was sworn in

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Mary Peltola wore the traditional footwear of the Yup'ik people when she was sworn in
Patriotism on their sleeves
Other candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.
While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.
In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.
She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June.
The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard.
"Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says.
"It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ashley Hinson's campaign style is inspired by the American flag

blocks.text: Ashley Hinson's campaign style is inspired by the American flag

Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial.
"Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."
Tie off, cowboy boots on

Once a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.
On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Despite political differences, Talarico, left, and Paxton have similar wardrobes

blocks.text: Despite political differences, Talarico, left, and Paxton have similar wardrobes
"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway.
"The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."
Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas".
"Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations.
"Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Former US president George W Bush was a fan of cowboy boots

blocks.text: Former US president George W Bush was a fan of cowboy boots
Meanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front.
It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".

The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms.

"The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising.
"A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit.
"The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Paxton's watch and Four Seasons polo shirt drew criticism

blocks.text: Image source, Facebook/KenPaxtonTX
Paxton's watch and Four Seasons polo shirt drew criticism
Personal uniforms
A uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.
It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.
Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns.
Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator.
"I always saw pearls on her," he says.
"Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Marsha Blackburn has been wearing a consistent style for decades

blocks.text: Marsha Blackburn has been wearing a consistent style for decades
"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.

Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.
The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics".
The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Abdul El-Sayed calls his outfit "minimal look, maximal politics"

blocks.text: Abdul El-Sayed calls his outfit "minimal look, maximal politics"
It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says.
"The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."
Trump, master of the image

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump's suit and red tie is instantly recognisable

blocks.text: Trump's suit and red tie is instantly recognisable
Friedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump.
His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House.

"[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says.
"If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wear similar looks

blocks.text: Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wear similar looks
Whatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in.
"What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

articles.title: A top-secret spy mission, a decades-old scandal – and the Austin Powers-esque saga to lift the lid
articles.summary:
Rex Patrick’s latest transparency fight is over what he calls ‘most open secret in the history of Australian spying’ – maybe even the world

  • Get our

blocks.text: A campaign to uncover any documents relating to whether Australian spies bugged Timor-Leste to gain the upper hand in sensitive oil and gas negotiations will be a little less secret after a critical win by the former senator Rex Patrick.

The politician turned transparency advocate is trying to finally lift the lid on the top-secret mission in 2004 that became a public scandal years later after an ex-spy and a former attorney general attempted to mount a case in The Hague.
But the Australian government stands by its Glomar response – to neither confirm nor deny first that the bugging took place and second that any relevant documents exist.
On Friday, the administrative review tribunal (ART) ruled in Patrick’s favour, forcing the commonwealth to hold unclassified parts of the three-day hearing in late November in public.

Government lawyers argued the whole saga is so sensitive that even sections of the hearing open to the public should remain behind closed doors in case someone accidentally says something they shouldn’t.
Patrick told Guardian Australia the situation was a farce, arguing the bugging scandal is the “most open secret in the history of Australian spying”, maybe even the world.
A ‘very high-stakes’ game
Patrick’s bid to gain further insight into the affair began with a request for cabinet documents from 2004 held by the National Archives of Australia.
The Australian government’s position, along with the responsible agency, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (Asis), remains that any such documents cannot be publicly confirmed or denied.
Asis contends that alone the records could undermine national security and Australia’s standings with other countries.
The documents would relate to Australia’s strategy for settling how much of the Timor Sea it could maintain control over after Timor-Leste officially gained independence from Indonesia in 2002.
The negotiations determined the countries’ shared control over the Greater Sunrise gasfields, which hold resources estimated to be worth more than $50bn.

Patrick’s win on Friday means at least some of the government’s defence over why it cannot publicly reveal details of the 2004 bugging – which preceded to a commercially favourable agreement for Australia against the impoverished nation – will be heard in public.

At a preliminary ART hearing last week to rule on whether part of the hearings should remain open, lawyers for the archives argued the matter is so sensitive that even sections of the hearing open to the public should remain behind closed doors in case someone accidentally says something they shouldn’t.
Parts of the hearing will already remain closed so top-secret details can be debated, but the commonwealth had argued the open hearings should also be debated in secret.

The commonwealth unsuccessfully proposed the media and the public should be barred from the open hearings but would be able to view a transcript after careful review by the nation’s foreign intelligence agency.

The deputy chief solicitor, Justin Davidson, argued last Thursday the stakes are “very high” and it would be nearly impossible to mitigate the risk of an intelligence official revealing something they shouldn’t.
“I’m not, frankly, beyond making a mistake,” Davidson said.

Ewan McMillan, an Asis deputy director general, and Michelle Chan, a deputy secretary at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat), will offer their testimonies in late November when the case is heard in full.
Davidson had argued the unclassified details they share in an open hearing might be “interesting to the public” but not necessarily in the public interest.

On Friday, the ART deputy president Peter Britten-Jones ruled against the commonwealth, noting officials were “highly qualified and experienced” enough not to let national secrets slip in an open forum.
“The risk of an inadvertent disclosure of certificated material is negligible,” he wrote in his ruling.
after newsletter promotion
Patrick said the whole administrative saga felt like a replay of an Austin Powers movie.
“Only Asis and Dfat think the operation is still a secret,” Patrick said.
“It’d be funny if it wasn’t so serious, or if the taxpayer wasn’t paying for the silk, barristers and lawyers arguing the government’s case.”
A decades-long international affair
Patrick’s latest push to reveal historical documents, or at least the existence of them, comes after years of attempts.

In 2021, the former senator took the archives to the tribunal for heavily redacting a cabinet submission from 2000 outlining Australia’s negotiating strategy for bartering with its impoverished ally on the Timor Sea maritime boundary and a related minute.
The negotiations, which predated the bugging scandal by four years, were critical for Timor-Leste and Australia, because they dictated access to the Greater Sunrise gasfields.

The tribunal later released the document with fewer redactions, which showed cabinet in 2000 was concerned that Timor-Leste’s independence process may disrupt access to the oil and gas reserves in the Timor Sea, because Australia’s prior agreement with Indonesia for a 50/50 revenue split would be void.

The bugging operation occurred in 2004 when Asis operatives planted listening devices in key Timor-Leste government offices to uncover Timor-Leste’s bottom line, its negotiating tactics and the competing views of cabinet members.

In 2006, Australia ended up securing a 50/50 split of the Greater Sunrise fields, positioned 450km north-west of Darwin and 150km south of Timor-Leste. The deal was a boon for the joint venture of multinationals, led by Woodside, seeking to exploit the Timor Sea.

The bugging operation was later revealed after a former Asis officer, known as Witness K, approached the lawyer and former ACT attorney general Bernard Collaery, who was also acting for Timor-Leste, in 2013 about his knowledge of the operation.

Together, the two attempted to help Timor-Leste’s dispute against the maritime boundary agreement in The Hague, the international permanent court of arbitration, before Collaery’s office was raided and Witness K’s passport seized.
Timor-Leste withdrew its Australian espionage claims in The Hague in 2017 as a “confidence-building measure”, and a new maritime border was signed in 2018.

In a 2019 affidavit for the proceedings against Collaery, which were dropped in 2022, the Timor-Leste president, Jose Ramos-Horta, said he believed the disclosure of further details of the operation would not create any new or additional problems for Australia.

“I believe the relationship between Timor-Leste and Australia would benefit from, rather than be prejudiced by, a full and open disclosure in this of what may or may not have occurred in 2004,” he said.

articles.title: Decision clearing path for Russia to join world juniors in Alberta is 'very unwelcome,' minister says
articles.summary: Canada's foreign affairs minister says the decision to let Russia back into the ice hockey world championships came as a "great disappointment" on Friday, as the country's ongoing invasion of Ukraine…

image.caption: Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand, seen in Toronto last month, says the government is still assessing the ruling from the Court of Arbitration for Sport that will allow Russian athletes to compete at the hockey world championships. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada

Canada's foreign affairs minister says the decision to let Russia back into the ice hockey world championships came as a "great disappointment" on Friday, as the country's ongoing invasion of Ukraine stretches toward its fifth year.
Anita Anand says 'all options are on the table' for Canada before hockey championship

Minister Anita Anand said the Canadian government is still assessing the ruling from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but said she was "not comfortable" with potentially allowing a Russian team to attend this year's World Junior Ice Hockey Championships in Alberta.

"Make no mistake, this is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," Anand told CBC's Power & Politics. "All options are on the table and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."
'Focus on the substance' of Canada and EU's partnership, not the name: Anand

items: Russia is back in the hockey world championships after sports court ruling

blocks.text: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) cleared the path on Friday for Russia to return to the ice hockey world championships, overturning an exclusion in place since the country invaded Ukraine in early 2022.

The court's ruling overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions, which had banned Russia and Belarus from international tournaments since Feb. 28, 2022. The federation, while disappointed with the decision, said on Friday it would "act in accordance" with the ruling.
This year's world juniors are scheduled for Dec. 26, 2026, to Jan. 5, 2027, in Alberta in Red Deer and Edmonton.
Ministers boycott group photo with Russian counterpart at G20

Also on Friday, the United States cancelled a traditional group photo the G20 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Atlanta after several European officials threatened to boycott the picture over the inclusion of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

In her interview, Anand said she was going to miss the picture because she was on a flight to the Canada–EU summit in Montreal, but, had she been there, she said she would've joined her fellow ministers in skipping the picture in protest.
"It is not my preference at all to be in a picture with Sergey Lavrov," she said. She added that she ultimately sat across from the Russian minister once meetings got underway.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, centre, attends the G20 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Atlanta on Friday. (Megan Varner/Pool/The Associated Press)
From her seat, Anand said she looked the Russian minister "straight in the eye" and told him Russian's ongoing attacks in Ukraine are "absolutely reprehensible and contrary to international law."

Some G20 countries had already expressed concern at the U.S. having invited Russia to the meetings, especially after U.S. President Donald Trump drove his administration's relationship with Ukraine to deeper lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.
The Canadian government has expressed solidarity with Ukraine from the outset and the two countries declared a 100-year partnership last month.

articles.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
articles.summary: Thailand has prosecuted 294 people since 2020 under its lèse majesté law, with sentences going up to 50 years.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020
ByJonathan Head
South East Asia correspondentReporting fromBangkok
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.

This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.

On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

blocks.caption: Image caption, A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prison

blocks.text: Image source, Arnon Nampa's family
A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prison

The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.

Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".

Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."

In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.

"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon at a protest in 2023

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Arnon at a protest in 2023
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children,

The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.

But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"

blocks.text: Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"

The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.

That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.

In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.

In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.

At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughter

blocks.text: Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughter
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.

A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.

She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."

In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.

"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020

blocks.text: Image source, Goodmondayshoot
Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.

She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.
"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."

She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.
Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"

blocks.text: A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"

Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.

But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.

"In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."
He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years ago

blocks.text: Image source, Arnon Nampa
Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years ago

As the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs.
This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.
The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.

The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom.

"Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.

Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

articles.title: Poland: Protesters clash with police over sacked court chief
articles.summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the firing of top court President Bogdan Swieczkowski as a move to "restore the rule of law."

image.caption: Donald Tusk's center-left governing alliance had vowed to reverse controversial PiS judicial reformsImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: Protesters gathered outside Poland's Constitutional Court on Friday night, with authorities sending police to the scene to secure the court's grounds.

It all comes after a statement appeared on the top court's website saying President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy had been suspended for one month. Fellow judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska will lead the institution during this period.
According to Warsaw police, officers responded to one judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff.
Tusk vows to 'restore rule of law'
Swieczkowski is one of a slew of politically aligned judges who were appointed by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move in a post on X.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," Tusk said.
"After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added.

blocks.caption: Officers responded to a judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staffImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: When Tusk's center-left alliance took over after the 2023 parliamentary election, the group announced it would reverse controversial PiS government reforms in the judiciary.
President cancels trip abroad
Right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki reacted to the situation by canceling a planned trip to Senegal.
"At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland," Nawrocki said.
But in recent months, Nawrocki had refused to swear in five top court judges nominated by parliament.
When these judges instead took their oath before parliament, Swieczkowski had denied them access to the building.

articles.title: Retired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freed
articles.summary:
Stephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’

In his first comments since recently being

blocks.text: In his first comments since recently being released from a Russian prison, a retired Michigan teacher said he only believed he would be freed when he got new clothes.

Stephen Hubbard, 74, remarked on Friday that he had heard many times previously that he would be released – but never really trusted what he was told, adopting a philosophy of “seeing is believing” and “actions speak louder than words”.

“Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison,” Hubbard said in his first public remarks since his 21 October release, which came during a visit at the White House with Donald Trump, “I went out and I saw the car, and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians, then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St Petersburg, ‘I’m really going somewhere.’”

Hubbard had been behind bars for more than four years on charges that he fought as a mercenary in Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022. His legal team has denied the Russian accusations and said he was not involved in any military activity.
Trump has previously said that he had asked Russian leader Vladimir Putin to free Hubbard – and that the US did not have to release anyone in return.
“He was somebody I wanted to get back,” the US president said as he hosted Hubbard on Friday in the Oval Office.
The White House allowed a limited pool of journalists into Trump’s meeting with Hubbard, allowing primarily news photographers and a television crew.

Many in the international community perceived Hubbard’s release to be Russia’s latest maneuver to bring Trump closer to Putin’s position on the war in Ukraine. It also offered Trump a diplomatic victory ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, when his Republican party is expected to lose seats in Congress.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

blocks.text: PITX: Bicol-bound bus trips continue despite Mayon eruption
Despite Mayon Volcano's eruption on Friday morning, bus trips bound for Bicol from the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) remain uninterrupted.

In a "24 Oras" report by Jonathan Andal on Friday, PITX said six out of every 10 buses bound for Bicol were already fully booked. However, walk-in passengers could still be accommodated on ordinary and air-conditioned buses with available seats.
While some Bicol-bound passengers expressed concern over Mayon's eruption, they still pushed through with their trips. Others, meanwhile, were unaware of the volcanic activity.
“Nakakapagalala kasi wala po kaming balita talaga na pumutok pala yung bulkan. Hangga’t mayroon pong bumabyahe, parang tutuloy po kami,” said Daisy Belga, a passenger bound for Albay.
(It's worrying because we had no idea that the volcano had erupted. But as long as buses are still operating, we will push through with our trip.)
“Kinakabahan, pero mostly kasi tagilid naman kami, [sa] Polangui. Medyo gilid man pero abot kami ng ashfall,” added Virgie Magalona, another passenger bound for Albay.
(I'm nervous, but we're somewhat off to the side in Polangui. Even though we're not directly in the affected area, ashfall can still reach us.)
In Andal's report, a bus company said its drivers traveling to Bicol had reported no problems along their routes. However, driver Lito Rodriguez said he would remain cautious.
“Medyo delikado. Magpapa-ano na lang, magpapababa muna ng abo,” Rodriguez said.
(It's somewhat dangerous. I'll just wait for the ash to settle first.)
PITX said buses with online reservation systems were already fully booked, but many buses without online booking options continued to operate even without full passenger loads.
Since October 25, PITX has recorded more than one million passengers.
The terminal's security personnel have also confiscated hundreds of prohibited items, including pointed objects and flammable materials.
Passengers heading to their hometowns brought various types of luggage, with some even traveling with their pets.
PITX said pets are generally allowed on buses with their owners, provided they comply with the requirements.
“Usually ina-allow ng mga buses natin. Dapat po may cage, vaccination card at siyempre diaper po,” PITX Deputy Spokesperson Kolyn Gervacio-Calbasa said.
(Our buses generally allow pets, provided they are in cages and have vaccination cards and diapers.)
Meanwhile, large crowds of passengers have also started gathering at the Five Star bus terminal in Cubao, Quezon City, with some trips bound for Cagayan already fully booked.

Victory Liner has increased the number of trips from Manila to Baguio to 250, up from 150, as it expects passenger volume on the route to double to 10,000 starting October 31. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/VBL, GMA News
Manila Port tightens safety measures for Undas 2026 amid passenger surge
Tighter safety measures are being implemented at the Manila Port amid this year’s exodus for Undas, following a RoRo vessel that listed to its right in Real, Quezon, on Friday morning.
In a "24 Oras report by Ian Cruz on Friday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) conducted thorough inspections at the port to ensure that cargo on the vessels is properly secured.

“Binigyan na po natin ng instruction ang ating mga inspector na busisiin nang maigi ‘yung mga cargo lalong-lalo na itong mga rolling cargo o mga sasakyan na sakay ng vessel, na siguraduhing nakatali at maayos dahil konting galaw lang po ng barko maaari po ‘yang mag-move at ma-outbalance ang barko pwede po siyang tumagilid,” Coast Guard Station Manila Deputy Commander P/Lt. Luther Quela said.

(We have already instructed our inspectors to meticulously check cargo—especially rolling cargo or vehicles on board the vessel—to ensure they are properly tied down and secured, because even a slight movement of the ship can cause them to shift, unbalance the vessel, and cause it to list.)
Several passengers at the port chose to travel by ship to save on fare and bring more luggage.
“Ang ticket namin for 3 pax nasa 12 [thousand] eh. On the way pa lang,” said Fatima Belarmino, a passenger bound for Cebu.
She added that traveling by airplane would require a budget of P10,000 per person.
Meanwhile, couple Rosanna Layson and Rick Moulton chose to take a ship so they could bring three carts of baggage to Palawan.
“Sa barko madadala namin lahat ng gamit namin sa bahay, durabox, mga chair. Hindi naman namin madadala lahat yan sa airplane,” Layson said.
(On a ship, we can bring all our household items, plastic storage boxes, and chairs. We wouldn't be able to bring all of that on an airplane.)
“Plane is quicker, that’s for sure, but it will be an interesting experience,” Moulton added.
Passenger turnout this year was lower compared to last year, according to the North Port manager. On Friday, passenger volume reached over 1,100.
At the Batangas Port, passenger numbers were also low. From midnight to 4 a.m. on Friday, only over 2,100 passengers arrived, alongside 358 rolling cargoes.
On Thursday, passengers departing from the Batangas pier reached 7,000, compared to 12,000 passengers in 2025.

“Matumal pa ang pagdating ng pasahero ngayon, compared noong isang taon. Nagmahal talaga ang pamasahe. Mauunawaan naman natin ang mga shipping lines because alam naman natin na mataas na ang presyo ng produktong petrolyo,” Batangas Port Manager Aurora Mendoza said.
(Passenger arrivals are still slow today compared to last year. Fares have genuinely increased. We can understand the shipping lines because we know that petroleum product prices are high.)
The PCG reminded the public that shipping companies do not allow the boarding of electric or hybrid vehicles on ships as part of heightened safety precautions. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan
articles.summary: Mary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting Republican
articles.byline: Lucy Campbell, Robert Mackey and agencies

blocks.text: The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot for US Senate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan.

Speaking at a news conference in Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman cited reporting by the New York Times which suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and national Democrats had, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”.
Both Dan Sullivans – one a Republican senator and the other a retired schoolteacher with no prior political experience – qualified for the ballot.
“We are taking that extremely seriously,” Heyman said.

“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” he added. “As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters.”

Separately, the Department of Justice on Friday asked a federal judge to issue a preliminary ⁠injunction ​that would ‌block ‌Alaska from ‌certifying its Senate election result if the incumbent senator loses to Peltola due to the presence of Daniel J Sullivan on the ballot.

Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into. It is highly unusual for federal prosecutors to confirm the existence of an open criminal investigation, much less discuss it publicly.
“The civil lawsuit is publicly faced, and is focused on preserving the ballots,” Heyman said, referring to a Department of Justice suit filed last week.
A day earlier, Peltola denied any prior knowledge of the alleged effort, telling supporters in Juneau, Alaska’s capital: “I am not interested in tricking voters.”

“I just want to clear the air,” the Democratic Senate candidate said on Thursday at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about.”

Peltola is running against Dan Sullivan, the two-term US senator. A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J Sullivan Jr as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.

The race is considered one of the most important contests of next week’s midterm elections, and will be key to determining control of the Senate. Alaska is one of a handful of states with Senate races this year that Democrats are targeting as they try to win back a majority in the chamber, where they hold 47 seats to the Republican party’s 53, and recent polls have shown Peltola in the lead.
More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke to the Associated Press. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.

Republicans have condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan, calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting the GOP candidate’s supporters.

Before the August primary, election authorities in the state attempted to disqualify the other Dan Sullivan, but the state supreme court ruled that he could appear on the ballot. Together with Sullivan and Peltola, the challenger was one of the top four vote-getters in the non-partisan primary.
after newsletter promotion
On the general election ballot, the senator will be listed as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the challenger “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”

Since the New York Times published its report, Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s Republican governor, separately announced plans to launch a criminal investigation, saying the story revealed “disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates – including one with the same name as an incumbent US senator – to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes”.

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the report “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Donald Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate if she won the election.
“Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for Darline Graham, a Republican senator, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted”.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
articles.summary: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.

blocks.text: The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
The latest move comes just days after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump, with the US president saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to try to end the war with Russia.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Zelensky said earlier this week that his country had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies.
And in a Telegram post late on Friday, the Ukrainian president reported that earlier in the day Russian ballistic missiles had struck two of the country's regions.
"They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," he said.
Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots, as Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.

It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
