articles.title: Victim of violent home invasion in Toronto's Bridle Path neighbourhood says family is 'traumatized'
articles.summary: The head of a Toronto real estate group says his family is traumatized and recovering after they were attacked in a violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood Thursday morning.

image.caption: David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, a real estate group, said his family is 'traumatized' after they suffered a violent and 'horrific' home invasion in their Bridle Path home Thursday. (macsuites.ca)

blocks.text: Toronto
The head of a Toronto real estate group says his family is traumatized and recovering after they were attacked in a violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood Thursday morning.
Toronto real estate CEO David Morton says his family members were shot, attacked with hammer

David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, said three members of his family are recovering in hospital after they were shot during the home invasion. All four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer, he said in a statement issued Friday.
"It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home," he said.
"No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives."

items: 4 hospitalized as Toronto police investigate home invasion, shooting at Bridle Path home

blocks.text: On Thursday, Toronto police said they responded to reports of a "violent home invasion" and shooting at a home on Hyde Park Circle near Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue E., around 3:43 a.m.

Police said three suspects, armed with handguns and a hammer, forced their way into the home through a rear entrance and attacked four adults in the home — a father, mother and their two adult daughters.
Two of the family members have life-altering injuries, police said.
Toronto police continue to investigate and are searching for three suspects.
Morton encouraged anyone with information to contact police.
Police are also urging anyone with information, dashcam footage or doorbell camera video to contact them.

articles.title: U.S. charges 5 more Canadians with voter fraud offences amid Trump administration crackdown
articles.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice says charges have been laid against five more Canadians for voting fraud-related offences, the latest in a flurry of similar prosecutions ahead of next week's midterm…

image.caption: The two women pictured are among at least 20 Canadians either charged with or sentenced for voting fraud-related offences in the U.S. this year. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement/U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. Department of Justice says charges have been laid against five more Canadians for voting fraud-related offences, the latest in a flurry of similar prosecutions ahead of next week's midterm elections.
At least 20 Canadians now charged or sentenced in U.S. election integrity investigations this year

According to a tally compiled by CBC News, at least 20 Canadians have now been either charged or sentenced in the U.S. this year in federal election integrity investigations. Most charges have been filed since last month, with allegations typically dating back several years.

The five latest cases were announced in a series of news releases Thursday and Friday from U.S. attorney's offices in Missouri, Tennessee, North Carolina and Wisconsin. They all involve Canadians living in the U.S. — most of them listed as lawful permanent residents — accused of falsely claiming citizenship to cast a ballot, or illegally voting in a past election.
The defendants are between 58 and 68 years old, according to the Department of Justice.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference

blocks.text: "The right to vote is fundamental to American citizenship and a cornerstone of our republic," Dan Bishop, the U.S. attorney for the Middle District of North Carolina, said in a statement.
Bishop said the recent charges "serve notice that those who violate our election laws, including non-citizens who register and vote, will be investigated and prosecuted."

A 69-year-old Canadian woman charged with 'illegal voting by an alien' was arrested after dark while in her housecoat, according to this image released by U.S. authorities. (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

U.S. federal prosecutors and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — have in recent weeks repeatedly highlighted their efforts to crack down on voter fraud.
"Anyone who unlawfully votes will be found and brought to justice!" HSI said Friday in a post on X.
U.S. authorities have announced similar charges against citizens of several other countries including Australia, Colombia, Cuba, Jamaica and the United Kingdom.

items: U.S. officials accuse Canada of midterm meddling — but Trump has endorsed foreign candidates

blocks.text: The efforts align with U.S. President Donald Trump's long-running false claims of widespread voter fraud in federal elections.
"The timing tells us why it's likely they're doing this," said David Becker, executive director of the non-partisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, in a recent interview.
He insisted what little non-citizen voting occurs in the U.S. has not affected the outcomes of elections.
Canadians sternly warned to stay out of U.S. elections as arrests ramp up
"This is likely an attempt to try to sow doubts about the election, in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.
Last week, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa said in a statement Canadians account for the "second highest total of prosecutions for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country."

items: U.S. 'monitoring' Canada for signs of midterm election interference, ambassador says

blocks.text: The embassy pointedly warned "all Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections."

articles.title: Alberta separatist Jeff Rath kicked out of governing United Conservative Party
articles.summary: In an email, the party's executive director said Rath had "made clear" he did "not support" the party.

image.caption: Jeffrey Rath, co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project, speaks to journalists at a referendum watch party in Edmonton, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
In an email, the party's executive director said Rath had "made clear" he did "not support" the party.
In an email, the party said he had 'made clear' he did 'not support' party
Separatist leader Jeff Rath, who rose to prominence in the lead-up to the Alberta referendum in his white cowboy hat, has had his membership revoked by the governing United Conservative Party.

In an email sent to Rath on Thursday and viewed by CBC News, Dustin Van Vugt, the party's executive director, said that Rath's "words and actions have made clear" that he does not support the party or its objectives.
"Your public conduct in relation to our party and leader has not met the basic standard of decency we expect of our members when they disagree or otherwise."
His membership was revoked immediately, Van Vugt wrote.
In a phone call, Rath said he knew why he was being singled out.
"Because I'm a very loud and effective critic of Danielle Smith," he said.
"She obviously does not want free speech in the party."
Rath said he also received an email from the UCP notifying him the party had refunded the $239 he paid in order to attend next month's AGM.
Rath and Smith have publicly sparred over their differing views on Alberta’s place in Confederation, and their debates have occasionally veered into more personal territory.

Earlier this week, Rath accused Smith of colluding with federalist leader Thomas Lukaszuk in a text exchange he posted online. When NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi questioned Smith about it, the premier noted Rath’s prior financial contributions to the Opposition party.
Speaking to reporters Friday, Smith confirmed the party's executive director had pulled Rath's membership.
"He’s never supported me ... He never supported me during the leadership, he never supported me in my time in office, and he certainly doesn’t support me now," she said.

"That’s irrelevant," she added. "What is relevant is that he has said publicly things like he wants to come to the AGM to turn the UCP into an independence party. And we are not an independence party."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alex Boyd is a senior reporter based in Calgary, interested in politics, provincial affairs and misinformation. She is a former national and investigative reporter for the Toronto Star. Reach her at alex.boyd@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term…

image.caption: Carney told DW that in 'many cases' there could be scope for deeper Canada-EU cooperation than between Canada and the USImage: Dmytro Rusanov/DW

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.

Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.

"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.
Canada is too reliant on the United States, Carney tells DW
What did Carney say about EU talks and closer ties to the bloc?
An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.

They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.

"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.

"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.

blocks.caption: Carney and EU leaders met at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal this weekImage: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What scope for EU-Canada cooperation does Carney see?

Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.

"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."

He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.
But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

blocks.caption: Carney said that, like von der Leyen but possibly unlike Germany's Friedrich Merz, he uses the term associate membership to describe the status Canada seeksImage: Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is Canada concerned the talks could alienate the US, or Trump?

Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.

"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.

Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."
But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.

blocks.caption: Carney has been in the midst of difficult trade talks with Donald Trump, who has at times shown his dissatisfaction with his neighbor to the north as only he can Image: Dmytro Rusanov/DW

blocks.text: He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."
Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."
"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."

Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.
"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.
Are the EU and Canada moving closer?
DW's Katharina Kroll conducted the interview in Montreal.

articles.title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of Poland's top court
articles.summary: It comes after the government suspended two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.

blocks.text: In a social media post, the Constitutional Tribunal wrote that the two men were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said his government was acting to restore the rule of law.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.
The Constitutional Tribunal was the spark that triggered Poland's long-running rule of law dispute after the PiS-led government took office in 2015.
The PiS majority in parliament quickly moved to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Tribunal was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Taking office in 2023, Tusk vowed to depoliticise the judiciary - but he has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.

Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Tribunal, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.

"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Tribunal by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine: Oleshky residents evacuate war-ravaged city
articles.summary: Under the local ceasefire, an aid convoy of 25 buses arrived with humanitarian aid and as transport for fleeing Oleshky residents. The Ukrainian city has been occupied by Russia since 2022 and faces…

image.caption: The Red Cross is on the ground in Oleshky assisting residentsImage: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, evacuated the war-torn city on Friday.
The evacuations come in the fourth day of a ceasefire in the city, the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine over four years ago.
The local ceasefire was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV also participated in deliberations with Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Under the ceasefire deal, an aid convoy of 25 buses, some ambulances, trucks and other vehicles arrived in the city earlier on Friday to deliver food and medicine to residents.
Demining operations preceeded the aid convoy's arrival, with a Russian sapper and one other person killed in the process.
Officials from both Ukraine and Russia came to gether in the rare joint humanitarian effort, which is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
How did the evacuations take place?

According to the plan, an estimated 2,000 remaining Oleshky residents were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian-held territory, Russian-held territory, or to remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

If residents chose to go to Ukraine, they would travel 450 kilometers (280 miles) through Russian-held Crimea to reach the city of Anapa in southern Russia. Then they would fly to Belarus before crossing the border into northern Ukraine.
Russia's lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses would transport residents who want to live in Russia.
It remained unclear how many people chose to leave the city, but Melania Trump posted on social media that the convoy had safely evacuated more than 750 people.
Aid convoy reaches frontline town of Oleshky
Harrowing conditions
Oleshky residents have spoken of the harrowing conditions they have had to suffer in the city, such as traveling along mine-strewn roads in search for food and water.
"The problem is that a lot of people are staying," one woman told Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
"I've been told that it's their own choice," Lubinets replied. "At the very least, we'll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through."
Lubinets was in charge of coordinating the operation with Lantratova.
The pair appeared side by side to address reporters and were cordial to one another, something not seen between Russian and Ukrainian officials since the start of the war.

articles.title: Some Backstreet Boys fans consider refund after Live Nation relocates them to cheaper, still-obstructed seats
articles.summary: Some Backstreet Boys fans attending one of the group’s Toronto shows aren’t happy with their seat change after Live Nation relocated fans who unknowingly bought tickets that had an obstructed view.

blocks.text: Toronto
Some Backstreet Boys fans attending one of the group’s Toronto shows aren’t happy with their seat change after Live Nation relocated fans who unknowingly bought tickets that had an obstructed view.
Ticketmaster failed to indicate their seats had an obstructed view during presale period
These Backstreet Boys fans say their 'obstructed view' seats were relocated to worse spots
Betsabe Bustillos from Welland, Ont., said she originally bought four seats in the second row of section 130 at Toronto's Rogers Centre during the presale period for around $1,300.

Days after the presale ended, dozens of fans flooded social media with complaints that Ticketmaster failed to indicate their seats had an obstructed view and that after the presale, similar seats were selling for a discounted price. That prompted calls for the vendor to issue an apology and rectify the problem, either through refunds or exchanges for different seats.

items: Live Nation to relocate Backstreet Boys fans who say they got 'screwed' on seats with obstructed views

blocks.text: After seeing the reports on social media, Bustillos said she checked her own tickets, which, much to her surprise, had also been marked as partially obstructed. She says she then reached out to Ticketmaster, where she was told she would be relocated to an unobstructed seat.
Instead, Bustillos says she was moved to a row much farther back and the view from her new seats is also obstructed.
"This is insane," she said. "It's destroying the entire experience."
In a statement to CBC Toronto Thursday, Live Nation spokesperson Shabnum Durrani apologized for the situation. (Paul Sakuma/The Associated Press)
Rogers announced earlier this month that it was the organizer bringing the Backstreet Boys to Toronto in 2027. Its announcement offered Rogers customers "exclusive" access to the Oct. 5 presale.
Live Nation oversees the concerts, and its subsidiary, Ticketmaster, operates the ticketing platform.
'There is no option at all': ticket holder
The Backstreet Boys are expected to play 12 shows across four consecutive weekends in Toronto, from February to March 2027.
In a statement to CBC Toronto Thursday, Live Nation spokesperson Shabnum Durrani apologized for the situation.

"We are always happy to work directly with fans to review individual concerns and explore available options," Durrani said. "We understand this has been frustrating and appreciate the patience of fans as we work to resolve these issues."

items: Live Nation, Ticketmaster vow to fight breakup after monopoly verdict
Backstreet Boys add multiple dates to planned Toronto concerts

blocks.text: Bustillos says a couple of friends backed out after they found out about the issues, meaning she was forced to sell two of the tickets. But she said she was really excited, which is why she’s not keen on a refund.
"That's not my goal. I want to go and I want to enjoy the concert," she said. "It's not great that we have to do all this work for something that we already paid for."
Bustillos says she will need to give Ticketmaster a response on whether she wants a refund or a relocation by Nov. 22.
"There is no option at all," she said. "You go with this bad view or you don't and you stay home."
The Backstreet Boys are expected to play 12 shows across four consecutive weekends in Toronto, from February to March 2027. (backstreetboys.com)
"If I don't get the solution that is fair for me as a purchaser, as a buyer, for this ticket, I will definitely get a refund and not go and miss it, unfortunately," Bustillos added.
Customer hoped for more solutions

Backstreet Boys fan Giulianna Heto said she was also blindsided by the partially obstructed seating. She told CBC Toronto Friday she had to talk to three different people before she finally spoke with someone at Ticketmaster willing to help her with her two tickets. But the suggestion was far from ideal, Heto says.
"It came to, 'Oh, you should list it, sell it to get your money back,'" she said. "I was told several times in that call to lie and to not mention that it was obstructed."
"That's pretty crazy," she added. "It's not fair."

Heto says some of the solutions she would have appreciated include an ability to pick her new seating, a chance to change the date she’d be attending or a difference in the price between her old and new tickets.
"It should have been announced [as] obstructed. There's other concerts that were," she said. "I just want Ticketmaster [to] take ownership for it."
In a statement Friday, Durrani said the Ticketmaster team connected with Heto Thursday night and are "working with her to explore available options."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Gabriela Silva Ponte has been with CBC Toronto since January 2025. Currently, she works as a web writer, but has previously taken on a variety of reporting roles in ethnic media newsrooms and at Toronto Metropolitan University. Gabriela graduated from TMU with a Bachelor of Journalism. You can reach her at gabriela.silva.ponte@cbc.ca.
With files from Kirthana Sasitharan, Tyler Cheese

articles.title: Tech sell-off deepens, sending Wall Street toward its worst day since June
articles.summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed about 3 per cent by mid afternoon. In Canada, the S&P/TSX composite index was down about 2.3 per cent. Worries are rising about whether the hundreds of billions of dollars…

image.caption: Tech stocks in North America slid on Friday due to AI worries. (Paige Taylor White/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New

The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed about 3 per cent by mid afternoon. In Canada, the S&P/TSX composite index was down about 2.3 per cent. Worries are rising about whether the hundreds of billions of dollars invested in AI will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it.
In Canada, the S&P/TSX composite index was down about 2.3%
A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street's frenzy around AI sent prices too high.

The S&P 500 dropped 1.9 per cent and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The Nasdaq composite was likewise heading toward its worst day since June, as the weakness for technology stocks dragged it down 3.1 per cent, as of 1:20 p.m. Eastern time. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down one per cent.
Canada's main index, the S&P/TSX composite, dropped about 2.3 per cent mid afternoon.

Intel's stock led the way lower and is flirting with its worst day since 1974 after tumbling 30 per cent. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts' expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Amazon sank 2.1 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon's reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion US of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion US on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.
How Anthropic's IPO creates a single 'God share' | About That

A day earlier, Alphabet's stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and almost single-handedly dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centres have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centres.
"We're moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the 'show me' phase," said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.
A drop of 4.8 per cent for the stock price of Nvidia, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 US from more than $86,000 US earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion US worth of crypto at Binance.
Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell.
If the AI bubble pops, will the whole U.S. economy go with it? | About That
ExxonMobil climbed two per cent, and Chevron added 1.7 per cent after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.

Mondelez International rose 3.9 per cent due to better than expected growth and Colgate-Palmolive climbed 3.6 per cent after higher prices for its products helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.

Expectations are high for U.S. companies' ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of a safer option. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Europe following sharper swings in Asia. South Korea's Kospi dropped due to AI worries, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng climbed slightly.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: ‘Deepest possible partnership’: Canada and EU announce new alliance
articles.summary:
Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’

Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded…

blocks.text: Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.

Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.

“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.

As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.

While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.
Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.

Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.

Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.
“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.
Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.

In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.

“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.
“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.

The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.
“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.

European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.
Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.

Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.

“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.

He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

articles.title: Truth Commission: Probe doctors who signed drug war death certificates
articles.summary: The Truth Commission wants five doctors who signed drug war death certificates investigated after alleged inconsistencies -- some bodies with gunshot wounds were deemed to have died from natural…

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 2:27am

The Truth Commission wants five doctors who signed drug war death certificates investigated after alleged inconsistencies — some bodies with gunshot wounds were deemed to have died from natural illnesses.
In a Friday report from Sandra Aguinaldo on What We Know So Far, the Truth Commission had 13 cases where the death certificates from the drug war contained false information.

The Truth Commission said that these bodies sustained gunshot wounds to the head and body, yet the death certificate listed illnesses such as pneumonia, heart attack, and sepsis as the causes of death.
The bodies of these 13 were exhumed and eventually analyzed by forensic pathologist Dr. Raquel Fortun.

The Truth Commission said that it will write to the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) and the Philippine Medical Association (PMA) to probe the five doctors who signed these death certificates.
The commission also plans to send these allegedly wrong death certificates to the two groups.
Families of drug war victims are also urged by the Truth Commission to come to them if their death certificates also listed a false cause of death.

“Pwede sila lumapit sa Truth Commission. May proseso kaming gagawin para ma-vet, ma-ascertain yung mga information na ganyan. Pwede sila matulungan kung paano, halimbawa, lumapit sa PRC para ma-correct nga yung record,” Commissioner Carlos Conde said.
(They can come to the Truth Commission. We have a process to vet, to ascertain information like that. We can help them, for example, on how to go to the PRC to correct the record.)

In a statement from the PRC, the agency said it took note of the Truth Commission’s call. Citing the “Professional Modernization Act of 2000”, the PRC said that Professional Regulatory Boards are allowed to investigate cases involving alleged violations by professionals.
The Truth Commission may also transmit these certificates and other pertinent documents to the PRC.

“The Commission, through the Professional Regulatory Board of Medicine, shall evaluate the available evidence to determine the appropriate action and assess whether sufficient grounds exist to proceed with the conduct of a motu proprio investigation,” the PRC said.
The Truth Commission may also file an administrative complaint before the Professional Regulatory Board of Medicine, together with the supporting evidence.

“If it is established by substantial evidence that the concerned doctors committed violations of the Professional Regulatory Law, the Code of Ethics of the Medical Profession, or other applicable laws, rules, and regulations, the Professional Regulatory Board of Medicine may impose the penalty of suspension or revocation of their certificates of registration to practice medicine in accordance with law,” the PRC said.

The PRC said that whether it acted on the basis of motu proprio or through a complaint, the investigation will follow applicable laws and rules, with respect to the rights of the concerned professionals.
At least 6,000 people were killed during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs. Human rights groups estimate that the number could reach as high as 30,000.
Duterte has since been arrested and detained at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, where he awaits trial for crimes against humanity. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
articles.summary: There is currently more irregular migration between eastern Libya and Crete, Greece. It's raising questions as to what connects people smugglers with powerful militias in eastern Libya and then in…

image.caption: A rescue of refugees in distress off the Libyan coastImage: Laurin Schmid/SOS MEDITERRANEE/picture alliance

blocks.text: This year, almost 20,000 people have already tried to make the perilous crossing from Libya in north Africa to the Greek island of Crete.
The route, which runs from the east coast of Libya to Greece, has become an increasingly significant corridor for irregular migration into Europe, Greek daily Kathimerini recently reported.
On Oct. 20 alone, Greek authorities registered 710 people in 14 boats. Hundreds more arrived the next day.

Many of the boats depart from areas around Tobruk, a port city on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast. According to Kathimerini, migrants pay as much as $4,000 (€3,600) for the crossing, which takes around a day and a half.
This particular route is becoming more popular in part because of crackdowns on alternative passages.
After eastern Libyan armed forces acted against people smugglers heading for Italy in 2023, the smuggling networks changed their methods, using smaller boats and sailing them towards Crete instead.

blocks.caption: Libyans protest against irregular migration in front of the International Organization for Migration office in Tripoli, June 2026Image: Mahmud Turkia/AFP

blocks.text: Fuelling the conflict economy

According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a think tank based in Switzerland, other groups have since entered the people smuggling business too, including those who previously mostly moved goods, vehicles or drugs.
Human trafficking in Libya is closely connected with what is known as the "conflict economy."

This sees armed actors gaining economic resources and political influence by controlling informal markets and transport routes. It also sees local power brokers using measures against smuggling to obtain financial or political support for themselves.
Social media's hidden role in human trafficking, smuggling

"Conflict and subsequent instability in Libya have created a fertile environment for migrant smuggling and TIP [trafficking in persons] activities to develop, in turn leading to the growth of smuggling in other locations along an established route," researchers at British think tank Chatham House wrote, after looking in depth at three different transit hubs across Libya. "This has led to an increase in the number of migrants entering Libya and the expansion of Libya's conflict economy."

"It remains the case that an entire business has developed around smuggling routes, regardless of whether that [smuggling] involves weapons, goods, people or drugs," Hager Ali, a researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, told DW.

If there are already contacts, transportation and security arrangements in place, then these can also be used for illegal activities like people trafficking, Ali said. Since 2014, Libya has been split into two. In the west, a United Nations-backed administration is based in Tripol; and in the east, in Tobruk, the second Libyan leadership is backed by former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar.

Haftar has managed to consolidate control over various armed militias, ruling with an iron fist. His sons also hold important positions. However, there are no proven links between the Haftars' networks and people smugglers on that coast.
But, as Ali explained, even the appearance of having some influence over these sectors can confer political influence.
"The more apparent control one has over this market, the greater one's influence," Ali told DW.

blocks.caption: A powerful and controversial figure in eastern Libya: Khalifa HaftarImage: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Those Libyans who can influence, or even prevent, departures are demonstrating their importance to other actors. For example, high profile operations against the smuggling networks can serve as a sign of political legitimacy. "They present themselves as somebody who can restore order and curb migration," Ali noted.

There's also increasing geopolitical competition in the eastern Mediterranean. In late October, the Tobruk government signed a maritime agreement with Turkey, a deal that Turkey had actually originally concluded with Libya's other government in Tripoli.

Turkey previously fought Haftar-sponsored militias during the Libyan civil war, and this deal represents rapprochement between the two. It is also a way for Turkey to get what it wants in a rivalrous situation in this maritime area — Greece rejects the agreement, saying that it infringes on Greek economic rights around islands like Crete and Rhodes.

A direct link between the new agreement and rising numbers of irregular migrants in Crete is not clear. However, Ali suggested that it wouldn't be inconceivable that irregular migrants could be used as leverage in these kinds of geopolitical conflicts.
European cooperation
The European Union has been cooperating with Libyans to prevent irregular migrants from getting to Europe — despite the Libyan actors' links to armed groups and their disputed political legitimacy.

There's an obvious contradiction in that, argued Andreas Dittmann, a retired professor from Giessen University and expert on human geography and development. Such cooperation between the EU and Libyans can serve as a control on irregular migration but it also adds to the Libyans' local power.

"If those in charge in eastern Libya are actually able to influence the scale and timing of such [migrant] movements, they're demonstrating their own strategic importance to European governments," Dittmann told DW.
A report by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, or IOM, illustrated how precarious the situation is for many migrants.

According to the report, which is based on data from May and June this year, around 950,000 migrants and refugees were registered as living in Libya. Many have only limited access to healthcare and tend not to have residence or work permits, all of which increases their dependence on informal markets as well as the risk of exploitation.
This story was originally published in German.

articles.title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme
articles.summary:
Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income

North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.

Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.

North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.

Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.

A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.

The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.

The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.

blocks.caption: Stolen funds are used to fund North Korea’s military, including its nuclear weapons programme. Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.

“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.

North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.

A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.

The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.

The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.

The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.

Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.

The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte won't attend fifth ICC status conference ahead of trial
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte will not attend the fifth status conference before the start of his crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published October 31, 2026 1:25am

Former President Rodrigo Duterte listens through headphones at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, The Netherlands on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 during the fourth status conference in his case. Screenshot from ICC livestream
Former President Rodrigo Duterte will not attend the fifth status conference before the start of his crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

In a document released on Friday, Duterte's counsel, Peter Haynes, said Trial Chamber III had granted the former president's request to waive his appearance at the November 2 status conference, allowing him to be represented by his lawyers.
Duterte previously attended the third and fourth status conferences.

The fifth status conference will tackle the list of witnesses, number of hours for the prosecution's presentation of evidence, potentially exculpatory evidence, agreed facts, as well as protective measures inside the courtroom, among other matters.

Duterte has been in ICC custody since March 2025 in connection with charges over killings during his tenure as Davao City mayor and in relation to the war on drugs during his presidency. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
articles.summary: European foreign ministers refused to be pictured with Sergei Lavrov at the summit being held in Atlanta.

blocks.text: Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.
One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What happens when Rodrigo Duterte's ICC trial opens on Nov. 30?
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court"s (ICC) trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte for crimes against humanity will open on November 30, with judges first asking him whether he admits guilt or pleads…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: The International Criminal Court’s (ICC) trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte for crimes against humanity will open on November 30, with judges first asking him whether he admits guilt or pleads not guilty.
In a media advisory released by the ICC Public Affairs Unit Friday, the ICC has laid out how the opening of the trial will unfold.
Will former President Duterte appear in person?
Under Article 63 of the Rome Statute, an accused person “shall be present during the trial.”
The ICC’s own Duterte case page likewise says the accused is expected to be present during trial, while any questions about how Duterte participates will be decided by the judges.
So far, Duterte’s defense team has made no public filing about how he will appear before the court on November 30.

In October, the ICC Registry advised judges to publicly explain any arrangement allowing Duterte to leave and re-enter the courtroom during proceedings, warning that unexplained absences could fuel disinformation among audiences following the trial from the Philippines.
The Registry noted that Philippine media were expected to follow the proceedings “very intensively” and pay attention to the “smallest details” of Duterte’s appearance and conduct.
It also said victims and affected communities placed “paramount importance” on Duterte’s presence during the proceedings.

The Registry further said that, if Duterte does not attend in person, participation by video link from the ICC Detention Center could be considered, subject to the Chamber’s approval. It said such an arrangement would still allow Duterte to communicate privately with his lawyers.
How can the public watch the conference?
Yes. The ICC will stream the hearing on its website, Facebook account, and YouTube Channel with a 30-minute delay.
Members of the public may also attend in person, subject to limited gallery space and a first-come, first-served policy.
What’s the hearing schedule like?
The hearing will begin at 10 a.m. in The Hague (5 p.m. Philippine time). Each hearing day is divided into four one-hour sessions:
10 a.m. to 11 a.m. (5 - 6 p.m. Manila)
3 p.m. to 4 p.m. (10:00 - 11:00 p.m. Manila)
The advisory said that the courtroom schedule may be adjusted “on a case-by-case basis,” meaning the exact timing will depend on how quickly the opening phase progresses.
What happens first?
According to the ICC Public Affairs Unit media advisory, Trial Chamber III will first verify that Duterte understands the nature of the charges before asking him to enter a plea.
The judges will then ask whether the former president makes an admission of guilt or pleads not guilty.
Who gives the opening statements?
The Office of the Prosecution will speak first, followed by the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV). The Defense may also give an opening statement if it chooses.
The prosecution has six hours total for its opening statement, while the CLRV has three hours. The statements will be delivered across the court’s four daily hearing sessions.
When will the first witness testify?
The first Prosecution witness is scheduled to start testifying following the conclusion of the opening statements, and the courtroom schedule will be adjusted on a case-by-case basis.
What charges does Duterte face?
Former President Duterte is charged with crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Rome Statute.
He faces three counts of the crimes allegedly committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population in the Philippines between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019:
Count 1: Murder as a crime against humanity in Davao City during his mayoral period, between 2013 and around June 2016
Count 2: Murder as a crime against humanity of ‘High-Value Targets’ in locations across the Philippines during his presidency between around July 2016 and July 2017.
Count 3: Murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity in barangay clearance operations in locations across the Philippines during his presidency between around July 2016 and September 2018.
Who are the judges?
The case is before Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou.
What happens after the prosecution case?
The hearings are scheduled to begin on 30 November 2026.
The Prosecution is currently expected to call a number of witnesses, after which the CLRVs may submit observations. The Defence will have the opportunity to present its case and call witnesses.
At the end of the trial hearings, the Trial Chamber judges will render their judgment within a reasonable period.
The judges will convict someone only if the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the charges have been proven beyond reasonable doubt.—LDF, GMA News
